Can an interface extend another interface, and can it have fields?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface, and when would you use each?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: An abstract class can hold state, constructors, and shared code but allows single inheritance; an interface defines a capability, allows multiple implementation, and since Java 8 can carry default methods.
tips: Give one concrete pair of examples (a family vs a capability) — it beats a list of differences.
Mention default methods explicitly so the answer does not sound pre-Java-8.
interviewQuestions.title: Abstract class vs interface

commonMistakes: Saying overriding is decided at compile time — it is decided at runtime from the actual object type.
Changing the parameter list in an override and accidentally overloading instead.
Narrowing the return type to an unrelated type, or making the overriding method more restrictive in visibility.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Overloading is several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in one class. Which one runs is decided by the compiler from the argument types — it is compile-time polymorphism. Overriding is a subclass replacing a parent method with the same name and the same parameters. Which version runs is decided at runtime from the actual object type — it is runtime polymorphism.

The rules differ too. An overload can change the return type and visibility freely, as long as the parameters differ; changing only the return type is not an overload and does not compile. An override must keep the same signature, may return a subtype (covariant return), cannot reduce visibility, and cannot throw new checked exceptions. Always write @Override on an overriding method: if you mistype the name or parameters, the compiler tells you instead of silently creating an overload.
followUps: Can you overload a method by changing only its return type?
Can a static method be overridden?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Overloading is same name, different parameters, resolved at compile time; overriding is a subclass replacing a parent method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.
tips: Say 'compile time vs runtime' first — that is the one line interviewers remember.
Mention @Override as a safety net against accidental overloading.
interviewQuestions.title: Method overloading vs overriding

commonMistakes: Assuming every bean is a singleton by design — singleton is just the default scope, not a guarantee of thread safety.
Expecting a prototype bean injected into a singleton to be fresh on every call — it is created once, at injection time.
Using request or session scope in a non-web application, where no request exists.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Scope controls how many instances of a bean the container creates and how long each lives. Singleton (the default) means one shared instance per container — the right choice for stateless services. Prototype means a new instance every time the bean is requested — the right choice for stateful, short-lived objects. In web applications there are also request (one per HTTP request), session (one per user session), and application scopes.

Two points catch people out. First, singleton beans must be thread-safe, because every request shares the one instance — keep them stateless or synchronise the mutable parts. Second, injecting a prototype bean into a singleton does not give you a fresh prototype per call: the container creates the prototype once, when it wires the singleton. To get a new one per use, inject an ObjectProvider or a Provider and call get() each time.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype bean inside a singleton?
Are singleton beans thread-safe?
interviewQuestions.question: What bean scopes does Spring provide, and which one is the default?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Singleton is the default (one shared instance); prototype gives a new instance per request, and web apps add request, session, and application scopes. Singletons must be thread-safe.
tips: Name the prototype-in-singleton trap — it is the most common follow-up to this question.
State the default first, then the others; interviewers check you know singleton is a default, not a law.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring bean scopes

commonMistakes: Saying BeanFactory and ApplicationContext are interchangeable — for most apps you want the ApplicationContext.
Manually creating a BeanFactory in application code instead of letting Spring Boot build an ApplicationContext.
Expecting lazy loading from an ApplicationContext, which eagerly creates singleton beans by default.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Both are IoC containers, but BeanFactory is the basic one and ApplicationContext builds on top of it. BeanFactory creates beans lazily — only when first requested — and offers just the core wiring. ApplicationContext eagerly creates singleton beans at startup, and adds the features real applications need: event publishing, internationalisation, resource loading, and integration with AOP and the web layer.

In practice, always use an ApplicationContext (Spring Boot creates an AnnotationConfigApplicationContext for you). Eager startup is a feature, not a cost: a misconfigured bean fails fast at startup instead of failing on the first user request. Reach for a plain BeanFactory only in a constrained environment, such as a tiny embedded tool where startup time and memory matter more than the extra features.
followUps: Which container does Spring Boot use?
Why is eager bean creation at startup a good thing?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext in Spring?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: BeanFactory is the basic, lazy container; ApplicationContext extends it with eager singleton creation plus events, messages, resource loading, and AOP/web integration. Use ApplicationContext.
tips: Frame eager startup as fail-fast — it turns a drawback into a design reason.
Name the concrete Boot container type if you can: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext.
interviewQuestions.title: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext

commonMistakes: Treating @SpringBootApplication as magic — it is three annotations combined, and you should know which three.
Putting the main class in the wrong package so component scan misses your controllers.
Adding @ComponentScan with a broad base package that picks up beans from another module by accident.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation that combines three others. @Configuration marks the class as a source of bean definitions. @EnableAutoConfiguration tells Spring Boot to configure beans automatically based on what is on the classpath. @ComponentScan tells Spring to find @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller classes in the current package and below.

The scan base matters: by default it is the package of the class carrying the annotation, so put your main class in the root package of your project (for example com.example.shop) so that com.example.shop.web and com.example.shop.service are all scanned. If a bean is not found at startup, a misplaced main class is the first thing to check. You can narrow or widen the scan with the scanBasePackages attribute, but the usual fix is to move the main class, not to add scanning config.
followUps: How does @EnableAutoConfiguration decide which beans to create?
What happens if two scanned classes define beans with the same name?
interviewQuestions.question: What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation do internally?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan — so the class defines beans, triggers auto-configuration, and scans its own package downwards for components.
tips: List the three annotations by name, then explain the package-placement consequence.
Mention the misplaced-main-class debugging tip — it shows real experience.
interviewQuestions.title: @SpringBootApplication internals

commonMistakes: Adding individual library versions by hand instead of letting the starter and its parent manage versions.
Including two starters that pull in conflicting versions of the same library without checking the dependency tree.
Treating a starter as a framework feature rather than a bundle of dependencies — it adds jars, not code.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
A starter is a pre-packaged bundle of dependencies for one job, with versions chosen to work together. spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson, validation, and an embedded Tomcat; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa brings Hibernate and Spring Data JPA; spring-boot-starter-test brings JUnit, Mockito, and AssertJ. You add one dependency instead of hunting down five compatible ones.

Versions come from the spring-boot-starter-parent (or the BOM): you declare the starter without a version and Boot supplies a tested one. That is why a starter keeps your build consistent — every starter in the same Boot release is tested against the same library versions. If you do hit a conflict, mvn dependency:tree shows which starter pulled in the unwanted version, and you override it with a property such as <jackson.version> or an exclusion.
followUps: What is the difference between spring-boot-starter-parent and spring-boot-dependencies?
How do you find which starter is pulling in a conflicting library version?
interviewQuestions.question: What are Spring Boot starters, and how do they simplify dependency management?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Starters are tested bundles of dependencies for one job (web, JPA, test); the starter parent supplies compatible versions, so you declare one dependency instead of many.
tips: Name three starters and what each pulls in — concrete examples beat a definition.
Mention mvn dependency:tree as the conflict-finding tool.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot starters

commonMistakes: Enabling every actuator endpoint in production, including env and heapdump, without security.
Assuming Actuator is on by default — only health and info are exposed over HTTP out of the box.
Checking only that the app starts, instead of checking /actuator/health in a deployment probe.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Actuator adds production-ready endpoints to your app for health, metrics, and inspection. The most used are /actuator/health (is the app and its database up?), /actuator/info (build and version details), /actuator/metrics (JVM, HTTP, and custom counters), and /actuator/env and /actuator/beans for debugging. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator, and in recent Boot versions health and info are the only endpoints exposed over HTTP by default — the rest need management.endpoints.web.exposure.include to be switched on.

Two habits matter. First, wire /actuator/health into your deployment: a load balancer or Kubernetes liveness probe should call it rather than just checking the port is open. Second, treat the detailed endpoints as sensitive: env can leak secrets and heapdump can leak memory contents, so expose them only on an internal port or behind authentication, never on the public internet.
followUps: How do you add a custom health indicator?
How would you secure actuator endpoints in production?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator, and which endpoints would you use in production?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Actuator exposes health, info, metrics, and inspection endpoints; use /actuator/health in deployment probes, and keep detailed endpoints like env behind authentication.
tips: Name the exact endpoints and the default-exposure rule (only health and info).
Mention the security warning — interviewers ask about it for actuator specifically.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Boot Actuator

commonMistakes: Calling DispatcherServlet 'the controller' — it is the front controller that routes to your controllers.
Forgetting that @RestController methods skip view resolution and write straight to the response body.
Describing the flow without naming HandlerMapping or ViewResolver — interviewers listen for both.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
DispatcherServlet is the front controller: every HTTP request enters through it, and it coordinates the rest. First it asks a HandlerMapping which controller method handles this URL. Then it calls that method (through a HandlerAdapter), passing in request data bound to method arguments. The controller returns either a view name plus a model, or — for a @RestController — a body object. In the view case, a ViewResolver turns the name into a template (such as a Thymeleaf page) and renders it with the model; in the REST case, a message converter serialises the object to JSON and writes it to the response.

So the short version is: DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → controller → (ViewResolver → view, or message converter → JSON). Exceptions anywhere in that chain can be handled centrally with @ControllerAdvice. If a request returns 404, the usual suspects are a wrong mapping, a controller outside the component-scan package, or a missing annotation — all of which sit on this path.
followUps: What is the difference between a filter and an interceptor in this flow?
Where does @ControllerAdvice fit into the request lifecycle?
interviewQuestions.question: Describe the lifecycle of a request in Spring MVC, starting at the DispatcherServlet.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: DispatcherServlet receives every request, HandlerMapping picks the controller method, the controller returns a view name or a body object, and a ViewResolver or a JSON message converter produces the response.
tips: Recite the chain as an arrow sequence — it is easy to follow and hard to get wrong.
Mention the 404 debugging angle: wrong mapping or a controller outside component scan.
interviewQuestions.title: DispatcherServlet request flow

commonMistakes: Returning a plain string from a @Controller method and expecting JSON — it is treated as a view name.
Putting @ResponseBody on every method instead of using @RestController on the class.
Using @Controller for a REST API and wondering why the response is a 404 for a 'view' that does not exist.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@Controller marks a class as a web controller whose methods usually return view names: return "home" and Spring resolves a template called home. @RestController is @Controller plus @ResponseBody on every method, so return values are serialised (usually to JSON by Jackson) and written straight to the response body instead of being treated as view names.

Use @Controller for server-rendered pages (Thymeleaf, JSP) and @RestController for REST APIs. The two are easy to confuse because they look identical — the difference is entirely in what happens to the return value. A common interview trap is a @Controller method returning a string like "success": Spring looks for a view named success and returns a 404 or an error page, while the same method in a @RestController would return the text success as the response body.
followUps: How do you return a specific HTTP status code from a @RestController method?
When would you use ResponseEntity instead of returning an object directly?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Controller methods return view names to be rendered; @RestController adds @ResponseBody to every method, so return values are serialised to JSON and written to the response body.
tips: Use the 'return "success"' trap as your example — it makes the difference concrete.
Say which one you use for APIs and which for pages; interviewers want the rule, not just the definition.
interviewQuestions.title: @Controller vs @RestController

commonMistakes: Extending JpaRepository when you only need basic CRUD — CrudRepository is the simpler, sufficient choice.
Calling save() in a loop for thousands of rows instead of saveAll with batching.
Expecting findById to throw when nothing is found — it returns an empty Optional.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
CrudRepository is the base repository interface with the basic operations: save, findById, findAll, deleteById, existsById, and count. JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository, which extends CrudRepository, so it has everything CrudRepository has plus JPA-specific operations: flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, deleteInBatch, and getReferenceById, plus paging and sorting through Pageable and Sort.

For a 0–3 year interview, the rule is simple: reach for JpaRepository when you need paging, sorting, or batch deletes; CrudRepository is enough for plain CRUD. Both give you derived query methods for free — findByEmail(String email) becomes a query from the method name alone — and both let you add @Query methods for anything the naming rules cannot express. One habit to build early: findById returns Optional, so handle the empty case with orElseThrow instead of calling get() blindly.
followUps: How do you write a custom query with @Query?
What is the difference between deleteAll and deleteAllInBatch?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between CrudRepository and JpaRepository?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: JpaRepository extends CrudRepository (via PagingAndSortingRepository) and adds paging, sorting, flush, and batch-delete operations; use it when you need those, CrudRepository for plain CRUD.
tips: Draw the hierarchy: CrudRepository → PagingAndSortingRepository → JpaRepository.
Mention the Optional return of findById — it is the detail that shows you have used it.
interviewQuestions.title: CrudRepository vs JpaRepository

commonMistakes: Putting @Transactional on a private method or calling it from within the same class — Spring's proxy never sees the call, so no transaction starts.
Expecting a rollback for a checked exception — by default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions.
Making every method @Transactional 'just in case', which hides real transaction boundaries and hurts performance.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
@Transactional marks a method (usually on a service) as one database transaction: either all of its writes commit together, or none of them do. If the method throws an unchecked exception (a RuntimeException), Spring rolls the transaction back; if it returns normally, Spring commits. That is the behaviour you want for a transfer that debits one account and credits another — a failure halfway must not leave the money debited but not credited.

Three rules decide whether it works. First, it only applies when the call goes through Spring's proxy, so annotate public service methods and call them from another bean — a private method, or a self-call inside the same class, runs with no transaction at all. Second, checked exceptions do not trigger rollback unless you set rollbackFor. Third, keep the transaction short and at the service layer, not the repository layer: a long transaction holds database locks and connections while your code does unrelated work.
followUps: Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
How do you make a transaction roll back for a checked exception?
interviewQuestions.question: What does @Transactional do, and when does Spring roll a transaction back?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Transactional runs a method inside one database transaction; it commits on success and rolls back on unchecked exceptions. It only works through Spring's proxy, so it needs a public method called from another bean.
tips: Lead with the money-transfer example — atomicity is easiest to explain with it.
Name the self-invocation trap: it is the most asked @Transactional follow-up.
interviewQuestions.title: @Transactional basics

commonMistakes: Saying a unique key cannot be null — it can, in most databases, and MySQL even allows several nulls in one.
Putting two primary keys on one table instead of one composite primary key.
Choosing a natural key (like an email) as the primary key when it can change — a surrogate id is usually safer.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Both enforce uniqueness, but they differ in three ways. A table can have only one primary key, and it can never contain null; a table can have many unique keys, and a unique column can usually contain null (MySQL allows multiple nulls in a unique column). A primary key identifies each row — it is the table's identity — while a unique key is an extra rule saying 'this value must not repeat'.

In practice: give every table a primary key (usually an auto-increment id), and add unique keys for business values that must be one-per-row, such as an email address. In MySQL's InnoDB, the primary key also decides how rows are physically stored (the clustered index), so lookups by primary key are the fastest access path, while unique keys get a secondary index.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL
);
```
followUps: Can a primary key be made of more than one column?
What is a foreign key, and how is it different from a unique key?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: One primary key per table, never null, identifies each row; many unique keys allowed, usually nullable, enforcing no repeats on a business value like an email.
tips: Give the three differences as a list: count, nulls, purpose.
Mention the InnoDB clustered-index point — it shows you know why the primary key matters for performance.
interviewQuestions.title: Primary key vs unique key

commonMistakes: Using HAVING without GROUP BY to filter rows — that is WHERE's job.
Putting an aggregate condition in WHERE, which fails because WHERE runs before grouping.
Forgetting that WHERE cannot see column aliases defined in the SELECT list in most databases.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has run. That ordering decides what each clause can express: WHERE can test plain columns but not aggregates, while HAVING can test aggregates such as AVG(salary) > 50000 but cannot cheaply test individual rows.

```sql
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'active'
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
```

Here WHERE first drops inactive employees, then GROUP BY forms one group per department, then HAVING keeps only departments whose average salary is above 50,000. A quick way to remember it: WHERE is a row filter, HAVING is a group filter — and any condition that mentions an aggregate function belongs in HAVING.
followUps: Can you use HAVING without GROUP BY?
Why does putting AVG(salary) > 50000 in the WHERE clause fail?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can test aggregates like AVG(salary).
tips: Walk through one query showing both clauses in order — it proves you know the execution sequence.
Use the memory hook: WHERE is a row filter, HAVING is a group filter.
interviewQuestions.title: WHERE vs HAVING

commonMistakes: Letting every client call services directly and duplicating auth, rate limiting, and routing in each client.
Treating the gateway as the place for business logic — it should route and protect, not implement features.
Forgetting the gateway is a single point of failure unless it is itself deployed redundantly.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
An API Gateway is the single front door for all client traffic. Instead of clients calling dozens of services directly, they call the gateway, which routes each request to the right service, and handles the jobs that are the same for every service: authentication, rate limiting, request logging, CORS, and sometimes response aggregation (combining calls to several services into one response for a mobile client).

That centralisation is the benefit and the risk. It simplifies clients — one base URL, one auth flow — and lets teams change a service's address or version without touching every client. But the gateway is now on the critical path for everything, so it must be fast, stateless, and run with several instances behind a load balancer; if it goes down, every service becomes unreachable even though the services themselves are healthy.
followUps: What is the difference between an API Gateway and a service registry?
How does a gateway differ from a load balancer?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the role of an API Gateway in a microservices architecture?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The gateway is the single entry point: it routes requests to the right service and centralises auth, rate limiting, and logging — but it must be redundant, since it is on the critical path.
tips: List the cross-cutting jobs (auth, rate limiting, logging) — that is what the gateway is for.
Name the trade-off in the same breath: single point of failure unless deployed redundantly.
interviewQuestions.title: API Gateway in microservices

commonMistakes: Running mvn install when you only meant to compile — it runs tests, packages, and writes to the local repository.
Using -DskipTests when you meant -Dmaven.test.skip: skipTests still compiles tests, maven.test.skip skips compiling them too.
Deleting the target folder by hand instead of running mvn clean, which is the repeatable way to get a fresh build.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
Maven builds run through lifecycle phases in a fixed order: validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy. Running mvn install executes every phase up to install: it compiles the code, runs the tests, packages the jar, and copies it into your local repository (~/.m2) so other local projects can use it. Running mvn clean first deletes the target directory, so nothing stale survives from the previous build — mvn clean install is the standard 'fresh build' command.

In this scenario, start by reading the failure, not re-running blindly. If a test fails, the build stops at the test phase and later phases never run — that is by design. Fix the failing test or the code it caught; only skip tests deliberately with -DskipTests (tests are compiled but not run) when you need a package urgently and understand the risk, and never skip them in CI. If the failure is a missing dependency, check the pom.xml: a dependency declared with the wrong scope (for example, test scope on a library used in main code) compiles in one place and fails in another. And if the build works for a teammate but not for you, delete target with mvn clean and check for a stale artifact in your local repository.
followUps: What is the difference between mvn package and mvn install?
What does -DskipTests do differently from -Dmaven.test.skip?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your teammate's Maven build works, but yours fails — and a full mvn clean install is the first thing you are told to run. What does that command actually do, and how do you diagnose the failure?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: mvn clean install deletes target, then runs every phase up to install (compile, test, package, install to ~/.m2). A test failure stops the build by design — read the failure, fix the cause, and only skip tests deliberately.
tips: Recite the phase order — validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy.
Name the two skip flags and their difference; it is the classic follow-up.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: diagnosing a failing Maven build

commonMistakes: Forgetting Java is pass-by-value and writing a swap on two int parameters.
Using the arithmetic version without mentioning overflow.
followUps: Why does swapping two plain int parameters inside a method not work?
When would the arithmetic swap give a wrong answer?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a method that swaps two integers without using a third variable. What is the catch with the arithmetic approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Swap with XOR (a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b) or with arithmetic (a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b); the arithmetic version can overflow, so XOR is the safer trick.
tips: Mention the overflow problem before the interviewer asks; it shows you know the trick is not free.
Point out that a temp variable is the right choice in production code.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: swap two numbers without a third variable

commonMistakes: Treating 1 as prime.
Looping all the way to n - 1 and calling it efficient.
followUps: Why is checking up to the square root enough?
How would you generate all primes up to n efficiently?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a method that returns true if a given integer is prime. How do you keep it efficient?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Handle numbers below 2 as not prime, then test divisibility only up to the square root of the number; if no divisor is found, it is prime.
tips: State the edge cases (0, 1, 2, negatives) before writing the loop.
Explain the square-root argument; it is the part interviewers actually test.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: check whether a number is prime

commonMistakes: Forgetting the base cases, which causes infinite recursion.
Claiming the naive version is efficient because it is short.
followUps: How would you make it linear with memoisation?
What breaks first for large n: time, stack, or integer overflow?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a recursive method that returns the nth Fibonacci number. What is wrong with the naive version?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Return n for 0 and 1, otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); the naive version is exponential because it recomputes the same values over and over.
tips: Name the repeated subproblems out loud before the interviewer points them out.
Offer the iterative version as the practical answer.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: Fibonacci series with recursion

commonMistakes: Sorting the string first, which works but costs O(n log n) for no reason.
Using nested loops, which is O(n squared).
followUps: How would you preserve the order of first appearance?
How would you find the first non-repeated character instead?
interviewQuestions.question: Write a method that finds the duplicate characters in a string. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Count how many times each character appears with a map, then return the characters whose count is more than one; it is linear time with one extra map.
tips: Say the complexity out loud: one pass to count, one pass to filter.
Use merge or getOrDefault instead of a manual containsKey check.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: find duplicate characters in a string

commonMistakes: Saying main can be overridden like an instance method.
Claiming the JVM calls any overloaded main.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Each word in the signature earns its place. public lets the JVM call it from outside your class, static lets the JVM call it without an object, void means it returns nothing to the JVM, and String[] args carries the command-line arguments. If main is not static, the JVM cannot call it and the program fails to start; if it is not public, older JVMs refuse to call it. You can overload main with other parameter lists, but the JVM only looks for the String-array version, so an overloaded main is just an ordinary method you have to call yourself. You cannot override main in a subclass in the polymorphic sense: a subclass can declare a static main that hides the parent's, but which one runs depends on the class you launch, not on the object type.
followUps: What happens if you run a class whose main is not static?
Can main be declared final or synchronized?
interviewQuestions.question: Why must main be public static void main(String[] args)? Can you overload or override it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The JVM calls main without creating an object, so it must be static and public; you can overload it, but the JVM only ever calls the String-array version, and you cannot override it because static methods are not polymorphic.
tips: Explain each keyword in the signature instead of reciting it.
Distinguish hiding from overriding for static methods.
interviewQuestions.title: The main method: signature, overloading, and overriding

commonMistakes: Comparing wrapper values with ==.
Using Integer in a tight loop and wondering why it is slow.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Java generics and collections only work with objects, so each primitive has a wrapper: Integer for int, Boolean for boolean, and so on. Autoboxing converts an int to an Integer automatically when you put it in a List<Integer>, and unboxing converts it back when you do arithmetic. The trap is ==: for wrappers it compares object identity, not value. Integer.valueOf caches -128 to 127, so Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; gives a == b as true, but with 1000 it is false, which is a classic interview gotcha. The other trap is unboxing null: Integer count = null; int x = count + 1; throws NullPointerException at runtime. Prefer equals for comparison, and avoid wrappers in hot loops because each box allocates an object.
followUps: Why does Integer.valueOf cache small values?
When would you deliberately use a wrapper instead of a primitive?
interviewQuestions.question: What are wrapper classes, and what goes wrong with autoboxing and ==?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Wrappers like Integer let primitives be used as objects in collections and generics; autoboxing converts automatically, but == on wrappers compares references, so use equals, and unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.
tips: Give the 127 vs 1000 example; it makes the == trap concrete.
Mention the null-unboxing NullPointerException.
interviewQuestions.title: Wrapper classes, autoboxing, and unboxing

commonMistakes: Returning a value from inside finally and overriding the real result.
Putting business logic in finally instead of only cleanup.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The point of finally is cleanup that must happen either way: closing a file, releasing a lock, returning a connection to a pool. It runs after a normal return, after a caught exception, and even after an uncaught exception propagates. The exceptions to the guarantee are cases where the JVM never gets to run it: System.exit() in the try block, a JVM crash, or the process being killed. A return inside try does not skip finally: the finally block runs before the method actually returns, and if finally itself returns a value, it overrides the try block's return, which is a bug magnet you should avoid. Since Java 7, try-with-resources is usually the better tool for closable resources because it closes them automatically and handles exceptions during closing properly.
followUps: What happens if both try and finally throw?
When would you choose try-with-resources over try-finally?
interviewQuestions.question: What does the finally block guarantee, and in what situations does it not run?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: finally runs after try or catch completes, whether an exception happened or not, so it is the place for cleanup; it does not run if the JVM exits, for example System.exit, or if the JVM crashes.
tips: Name the two real cases where finally does not run.
Mention try-with-resources as the modern alternative.
interviewQuestions.title: try-catch-finally: what runs, and when finally does not

commonMistakes: Using == to compare strings.
Creating strings with new String for no reason.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: When you write String a = "hello"; String b = "hello";, both references point to the same pooled object, so a == b is true. When you write new String("hello"), you force a new object on the heap even though an identical pooled one exists, so == is false while equals is true. The pool exists because strings are immutable and heavily reused, so sharing them saves memory. Strings built at runtime, for example by concatenation in a loop, are not pooled automatically; calling intern() on such a string adds it to the pool and returns the pooled reference. The practical rule is simple: always compare strings with equals, and never rely on == or on the pool for correctness.
followUps: What does intern() do, and when would you use it?
Why is immutability what makes pooling safe?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the String pool, and how does a String literal differ from new String("...")?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Literals are interned in the String pool, so equal literals share one object; new String always creates a fresh object on the heap, so == can be false even when the contents are equal.
tips: Use the literal-vs-new example to make the pool visible.
Always end with: compare strings with equals.
interviewQuestions.title: The String pool: literals versus new String

commonMistakes: Saying static methods can be overridden.
Accessing instance fields from a static method.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A static variable has exactly one copy shared by every instance of the class, which is why it is used for constants and counters. A static method can be called through the class without creating an object, but precisely because there is no object, it cannot touch instance fields or call instance methods, and it cannot use this or super. Static methods are resolved by the reference type at compile time, so a subclass that declares the same static method hides the parent's rather than overriding it: no polymorphism applies. A static block runs once when the class is first loaded, which is useful for one-time setup such as loading a driver or filling a lookup map. Common misuses are making everything static to avoid creating objects, which kills testability, and keeping mutable state in static fields, which becomes shared mutable state across threads.
followUps: Can a static method call an instance method? What has to change first?
When exactly does a static block run?
interviewQuestions.question: What does static mean in Java, and what are its limits?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: static belongs to the class, not to any object, so static members are shared by all instances; static methods cannot use this or super and cannot be overridden, only hidden, and static blocks run once when the class loads.
tips: Explain static as 'belongs to the class, not the object' first.
Contrast hiding with overriding.
interviewQuestions.title: The static keyword: methods, blocks, and what you cannot do

commonMistakes: Saying LinkedList is always better for insertions without mentioning the walk to the node.
Claiming either is thread-safe.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An ArrayList stores elements in a contiguous array that grows, usually by about half, when it fills up, copying the old contents over. Getting element i is a direct array lookup, O(1), but inserting or deleting in the middle shifts everything after it, O(n). A LinkedList stores each element in a node with links to its neighbours, so inserting or removing at a known node is just relinking pointers, O(1), but reaching element i means walking from the nearest end, O(n). In practice ArrayList wins for almost everything because it is cache-friendly and random access dominates; LinkedList is only worth it when you mostly add and remove at the ends, which is what a deque is for, and even then ArrayDeque is usually the better choice. Neither is thread-safe.
followUps: Why does ArrayList usually beat LinkedList even for frequent insertions?
What would you use for a queue instead of LinkedList?
interviewQuestions.question: How do ArrayList and LinkedList differ internally, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ArrayList is a resizable array: fast random access but slow insertion in the middle. LinkedList is a chain of nodes: slow random access but cheap insertion and removal once you are at the node.
tips: Lead with the internal structure, then derive the costs from it.
Mention ArrayDeque as the better queue.
interviewQuestions.title: ArrayList versus LinkedList: internals and when to use each

commonMistakes: Saying HashSet compares elements with ==.
Overriding equals without hashCode in a class used in a set.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Internally a HashSet keeps a HashMap where every element you add becomes a key and the value is a single shared dummy object. Adding an element calls put on the map; if the key is already there, put returns the old value and add returns false, so the duplicate never enters the set. Whether two elements count as the same depends entirely on equals and hashCode: if you override equals without hashCode, two equal objects can land in different buckets and both be stored, breaking the set. That is why the equals/hashCode contract matters in practice, not just in theory. HashSet makes no promise about iteration order, and it allows one null element.
followUps: What breaks if you override equals but not hashCode?
How would you keep insertion order in a set?
interviewQuestions.question: How does a HashSet ensure that it never contains duplicates?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: HashSet is backed by a HashMap: each element is stored as a key, and adding an element that is already present is rejected because the map already has that key, judged by equals and hashCode.
tips: Explain the HashMap backing first; the rest follows.
Tie it directly to the equals/hashCode contract.
interviewQuestions.title: How HashSet guarantees no duplicates

commonMistakes: Using TreeMap when no ordering is needed and paying log n for nothing.
Putting a null into a TreeSet and being surprised by the exception.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A HashMap stores entries in buckets by hash, so iteration order is unspecified and lookup is constant time on average. A TreeMap stores entries in a balanced red-black tree ordered by the keys, either their natural ordering or a Comparator you supply, so you can iterate in sorted order and ask for ranges like 'all keys below X'. That ordering costs O(log n) per get, put, and remove, and it means keys must be comparable: a null key throws NullPointerException when natural ordering is used, and a TreeSet has the same rule, which is why a TreeSet is the wrong choice when your elements can be null. The same idea applies to sets: HashSet for speed, LinkedHashSet for insertion order, TreeSet for sorted order.
followUps: How would you get all entries with keys in a range from a TreeMap?
What happens if you put a null key into a TreeMap?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose a TreeMap over a HashMap?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Choose TreeMap when you need keys in sorted order; it keeps them in a red-black tree at O(log n) per operation, while HashMap is unordered but O(1) on average. TreeMap also rejects null keys with natural ordering.
tips: Frame it as a trade: sorted order costs log n.
Mention the three sets together as a decision trio.
interviewQuestions.title: TreeMap versus HashMap: ordering, cost, and nulls

commonMistakes: Expecting filter or map to change the original collection.
Forgetting the terminal operation, so the pipeline never executes.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: filter takes a Predicate and returns a stream containing only the elements that pass the test, so the element type does not change: a Stream<String> filtered is still a Stream<String>. map takes a Function and applies it to every element, producing a new value for each one, so the type can change, for example Stream<String> to Stream<Integer> by mapping to lengths. Both are intermediate operations, which means they do nothing until a terminal operation like collect or forEach runs; that laziness lets the pipeline fuse the steps into a single pass and lets short-circuiting operations like findFirst stop early. A common beginner mistake is writing a stream pipeline with no terminal operation and wondering why nothing happened.
followUps: Why does a stream pipeline with no terminal operation do nothing?
How would you get the first matching element without processing the whole list?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between filter and map in the Stream API?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: filter keeps or drops elements based on a condition and returns the same type; map transforms each element into something else, possibly of a different type. Both are lazy intermediate operations.
tips: Use a one-line example of each side by side.
Stress that both are lazy until a terminal operation runs.
interviewQuestions.title: Stream filter versus map

commonMistakes: Using field injection, which hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
Making a required dependency optional through a setter.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: With constructor injection, every dependency is supplied when the object is created, so the object can never exist in a half-built state, the fields can be final, and a test can construct the object with plain new and pass in mocks. With setter injection, dependencies are optional and can be changed later, which is occasionally useful for optional collaborators, but it also means the object can be used before a dependency is set, producing a NullPointerException far from the real cause. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor is autowired automatically, so constructor injection needs no annotation at all. The Spring team and the community recommend constructor injection as the default, with setter injection reserved for genuinely optional dependencies.
followUps: How do you unit test a class that uses constructor injection?
When would setter injection actually be the better choice?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between constructor injection and setter injection, and which should you prefer?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Constructor injection passes dependencies through the constructor, making them required and the bean immutable; setter injection sets them after construction, making them optional. Prefer constructor injection.
tips: Lead with the guarantee: the object cannot exist without its dependencies.
Mention that a single constructor needs no @Autowired.
interviewQuestions.title: Constructor injection versus setter injection

commonMistakes: Assuming singleton scope means thread safety.
Storing per-request data in a bean field.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Singleton scope controls how many instances Spring creates, not how threads use them. In a web application, dozens of request threads call the same singleton service at the same time, so if that service keeps mutable state in a field, for example a counter or a list that accumulates results, threads will overwrite each other's data. The standard fix is to keep beans stateless: hold dependencies in final fields, keep all working data in local variables or method parameters, and pass state through method arguments instead of fields. If a bean genuinely needs shared mutable state, use thread-safe structures such as AtomicInteger or ConcurrentHashMap, or synchronise explicitly. A prototype-scoped bean avoids sharing, but it is not a cure-all: the prototype instance can still be shared if a singleton holds a reference to it.
followUps: How would you fix a singleton service that keeps a mutable counter field?
Does prototype scope guarantee thread safety?
interviewQuestions.question: Spring beans are singletons by default. Does that make them thread-safe?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: No: singleton only means one shared instance. The bean is thread-safe only if it is stateless or its state is properly synchronised; mutable fields shared across requests are a race condition.
tips: Separate the two ideas: one instance is not the same as safe sharing.
Give the concrete fix: stateless beans, local variables.
interviewQuestions.title: Are Spring singleton beans thread-safe?

commonMistakes: Hardcoding the port in code instead of configuration.
Assuming Tomcat is the only embedded server.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The embedded Tomcat starts on port 8080 by default. The usual way to change it is server.port=9090 in application.properties or application.yml, and the same value can come from an environment variable or a command-line argument, which is how deployments usually override it without rebuilding. Setting server.port=0 asks the operating system for any free port, which is handy in tests to avoid clashes. To switch the server, add a different starter such as Jetty or Undertow and exclude Tomcat; Spring Boot picks the server on the classpath. To run with no server at all, for example a batch job, set spring.main.web-application-type=none or simply leave out the web starter.
followUps: How do you find out which random port was assigned?
How would you run the same jar with a different port in production?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you change the port of a Spring Boot application, and can you run it without a web server?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Set server.port in application.properties or with the SERVER_PORT environment variable; set server.port=0 for a random port, and use spring-boot-starter without the web starter or spring.main.web-application-type=none for a non-web app.
tips: Mention the environment variable override; interviewers like deployment awareness.
Note that the server comes from the starter on the classpath.
interviewQuestions.title: Changing the port and the embedded server in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Returning 200 for everything and encoding errors in the body.
Returning a body with 204 No Content.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Returning a plain object from a controller always produces 200 OK, which is fine for reads but wrong for creations and deletions. ResponseEntity wraps the body with a status and headers, so you can say exactly what happened: ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved) returns 201 with a Location header pointing at the new resource, ResponseEntity.noContent().build() returns 204 for a DELETE, which has no body by design, and ResponseEntity.notFound().build() returns 404. The common mistakes are returning 200 for a creation, returning 200 with a body for a DELETE, and returning 200 with an error message instead of a 4xx code, which forces clients to parse bodies to detect failure. For errors, combine ResponseEntity with @ControllerAdvice so every failure path produces a consistent shape.
followUps: Why should a creation return 201 instead of 200?
How do you return a consistent error body for all failures?
interviewQuestions.question: What is ResponseEntity used for, and which status code should a DELETE return?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ResponseEntity lets a controller control the status code, headers, and body together; return 201 with a Location header for a creation, 200 for a successful read, 204 No Content for a successful DELETE, and 404 when the resource does not exist.
tips: Give the four codes as a small table in your head: 200, 201, 204, 404.
Mention the Location header on creation.
interviewQuestions.title: ResponseEntity and choosing the right HTTP status code

commonMistakes: Putting a resource identifier in a query parameter.
Forgetting that a missing required request parameter gives a 400.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Use @PathVariable when the value identifies the resource: GET /users/{id} with @PathVariable Long id. The value is required, because without it the URL does not match the mapping at all. Use @RequestParam for everything that modifies how you fetch or filter: ?page=2&size=20, ?status=ACTIVE, or an optional search term. Request parameters can be optional with required=false, can have a defaultValue, and are usually strings that Spring converts to the target type. A common mistake is putting an identifier in a query parameter when it belongs in the path, or marking a request parameter required when clients may legitimately omit it. Both annotations can appear in the same method, for example /users/{id}/orders?status=SHIPPED.
followUps: How do you make a request parameter optional with a default?
When would you use @RequestBody instead of either?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between @RequestParam and @PathVariable in Spring MVC?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @PathVariable takes a value from the URL path itself, such as /users/42, identifying a resource; @RequestParam takes a value from the query string, such as /users?page=2, usually for filtering, paging, or optional inputs.
tips: Give one URL that uses both, to show they compose.
Explain the rule: path identifies, query filters.
interviewQuestions.title: @RequestParam versus @PathVariable

commonMistakes: Using CascadeType.ALL on every relationship by default.
Confusing cascading with orphanRemoval.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Without cascading, saving an Order does nothing to the OrderLine objects in its list; you must save each one yourself. With cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST on the relationship, one save of the parent persists the children too, which matches how we think about an order and its lines as one unit. The cascade types mirror the operations: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH, and ALL for all of them. REMOVE deserves caution: deleting a parent silently deletes its children, which is correct for order lines but catastrophic for a shared lookup entity. orphanRemoval is related but different: it deletes a child when you remove it from the parent's collection, even without deleting the parent. A good rule is to cascade only along true ownership relationships, where the child has no life of its own.
followUps: What is the difference between CascadeType.REMOVE and orphanRemoval?
Why should you not cascade everything with CascadeType.ALL by default?
interviewQuestions.question: What is cascading in JPA, and when should you avoid CascadeType.REMOVE?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Cascading copies an operation on a parent entity to its children, so persisting a parent also persists new children; REMOVE is dangerous because deleting a parent deletes the children too, which is only safe when children cannot exist without the parent.
tips: Use the order-and-lines example; it makes ownership concrete.
Name the ownership rule: cascade only what the parent owns.
interviewQuestions.title: Cascading in JPA: what it does and when it hurts

commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN and silently losing unmatched rows.
Forgetting that the unmatched side comes back as nulls.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Imagine employees and departments. An inner join of the two returns only employees who belong to a department that exists, dropping anyone with a null or unmatched department id. A left join returns every employee, filling department columns with null where there is no match, which is exactly how you find employees without a department: left join and filter where the department key is null. RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image and is rarely used, since swapping the table order turns it into a left join. FULL OUTER JOIN returns unmatched rows from both sides, and CROSS JOIN produces every combination. The most common beginner error is using an inner join when the question needs the unmatched rows too, and silently dropping data.
followUps: How would you find all employees who have no department?
When would you use a FULL OUTER JOIN?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT OUTER JOIN?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables; LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and nulls for the right side when there is no match, so it also shows left rows with no partner.
tips: Use the employees-without-departments example; it is the standard follow-up.
Draw the two overlapping circles mentally: inner is the overlap only.
interviewQuestions.title: INNER JOIN versus OUTER JOIN

commonMistakes: Indexing every column and wondering why writes got slower.
Indexing a boolean column and expecting a big win.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Without an index, the database must scan every row to answer a WHERE clause. With a B-tree index on the filtered column, it walks the tree to the matching rows directly, which is the difference between milliseconds and seconds on a large table. The price is paid on every insert, update, and delete, because each index must be updated too, and each index consumes disk space. That is why you index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY, and why you avoid indexing low-cardinality columns such as a boolean flag, where the index rarely narrows anything down. You can check whether an index is actually used with EXPLAIN, and a composite index only helps when the query filters on its leading columns, in order.
followUps: Why is a composite index useless if you only filter on its second column?
How do you check whether a query uses an index?
interviewQuestions.question: What is an index in SQL, and when does adding one hurt?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: An index is a separate lookup structure, usually a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table; it speeds up reads and filtering but slows down writes and costs storage, so index columns you filter or join on, not every column.
tips: Always state both sides: faster reads, slower writes.
Mention EXPLAIN as the way to verify instead of guessing.
interviewQuestions.title: Indexes in SQL: what they speed up and what they cost

commonMistakes: Claiming microservices are always better.
Splitting services by technical layer instead of by business capability.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In a monolith, a function call is a function call: transactions are simple, debugging is straightforward, and deployment is one artifact. In microservices, every cross-service call is a network call that can fail, be slow, or return partial results, so you need service discovery, distributed tracing, eventual consistency, and deployment pipelines per service. The benefits are real: teams can deploy and scale services independently, and one service can fail without taking the whole system down. But those benefits only pay off at a certain size. For a small team or a product still finding its shape, a monolith, ideally a modular monolith with clear internal boundaries, is faster to build and easier to reason about, and services can be extracted later when a boundary proves itself.
followUps: What problems appear the moment you split a monolith in two?
What is a modular monolith?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a monolith and microservices, and when is a monolith the better choice?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A monolith is one deployable unit with all modules inside; microservices split the system into small independently deployable services. Microservices buy independent scaling and deployment but cost you distributed complexity, so a small team or a simple domain should start with a monolith.
tips: Lead with the cost, not the hype: every call becomes a network call.
Name the modular monolith as the sensible middle ground.
interviewQuestions.title: Monolith versus microservices: the real trade-off

commonMistakes: Calling run() and thinking a new thread was created.
Trying to restart a finished thread instead of creating a new one.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A new Thread object is in NEW until start() is called, which moves it to RUNNABLE, meaning it is ready to run or running. From there it can become BLOCKED while waiting for a monitor lock, WAITING while waiting indefinitely for another thread, for example in Object.wait() or join(), or TIMED_WAITING while sleeping or waiting with a timeout. When run() finishes, the thread is TERMINATED and can never run again: calling start() a second time throws IllegalThreadStateException. To run the same work again you must create a new Thread object, which is one reason executors are preferred: they manage a pool of reusable threads so you never deal with this directly. Also remember that run() and start() are different: calling run() directly just executes the method on the current thread, with no new thread at all.
followUps: What is the difference between calling start() and calling run()?
What puts a thread into WAITING versus TIMED_WAITING?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the states of a Java thread, and what happens if you call start() twice?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A thread moves from NEW to RUNNABLE to TERMINATED, passing through BLOCKED, WAITING, or TIMED_WAITING; calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a terminated thread cannot be restarted.
tips: Walk the states in order; interviewers often ask for them by name.
Call out the run-versus-start trap explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Thread lifecycle in Java, and why you cannot start a thread twice

commonMistakes: Saying objects are stored on the stack.
Saying the heap is faster than the stack.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Every thread gets its own stack, and every method call pushes a frame onto it holding local variables and the return address. When the method returns, the frame is popped, so stack memory is allocated and freed automatically and quickly, which is why it is faster to access. The heap is a single shared area where all objects live, including the objects that local variables point to. Heap memory is managed by the garbage collector, and running out of it gives OutOfMemoryError, while recursing too deeply exhausts the stack and gives StackOverflowError. Two related areas complete the picture: the method area, or metaspace, holds class metadata, and the program counter register tracks the current instruction. A classic follow-up is where a String literal lives: the object is on the heap, in the String pool, while the reference to it sits in a stack frame or another object.
followUps: What error do you get from infinite recursion, and why?
Where does a local variable's object live: stack or heap?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between heap and stack memory in Java?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The heap holds objects and is shared by all threads, managed by the garbage collector; the stack holds one frame per method call with local variables and is private to each thread, and it is faster to access.
tips: Contrast who owns each area: one stack per thread, one shared heap.
Pair each area with its error: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError.
interviewQuestions.title: JVM memory areas: heap versus stack
HashMap treeify rules
interviewQuestions.question: When does a HashMap bucket turn from a list into a tree?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: When a bucket's chain reaches 8 entries — but only if the table already has at least 64 buckets. With a smaller table, the map resizes instead. A tree shrinks back to a list at 6 entries.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Since Java 8, collisions in a bucket form a linked list that converts to a balanced red-black tree when the chain reaches 8 entries, so a bad hash degrades to logarithmic lookup instead of a linear scan. The conversion happens only when the table has at least 64 buckets: with a smaller table, resizing spreads the entries across more buckets and is the better fix. When removals shrink a tree bucket to 6 entries it converts back to a list — the gap between 8 and 6 is deliberate hysteresis, so a bucket hovering at the threshold does not flip on every insert and remove.
followUps: Why 6 for untreeify and 8 for treeify?
What does the tree compare when keys are not Comparable?
tips: Give all three numbers: 8, 64, 6.
Explain why the resize happens instead — the map is simply too small.
commonMistakes: Saying treeify happens at 8 unconditionally.
Forgetting the 64-bucket condition.

interviewQuestions.title: Is Java pass-by-value?
interviewQuestions.question: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Always pass-by-value: the argument's value is copied into the parameter, and for objects the value copied is the reference.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: When a method is called, each argument is evaluated and a copy of its value is placed in the parameter. For a primitive the copy is the value itself, so changing the parameter cannot affect the caller. For an object the copy is the reference — the method's parameter and the caller's variable point at the same object, so mutating the object through the parameter is visible, but reassigning the parameter only changes the local copy. That one sentence explains both observations that confuse candidates: mutation is visible, replacement is not.
followUps: Why can't you write a swap method in Java?
What happens if a method reassigns its object parameter?
tips: Lead with the one sentence, then give the mutation-versus-reassignment test.
Use the swap example — it is the standard follow-up.
commonMistakes: Saying Java is pass-by-reference because mutation is visible.
Saying primitives are pass-by-value but objects are pass-by-reference.

interviewQuestions.title: Why swap does not work in Java
interviewQuestions.question: Why can you not write a swap method for two objects in Java?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Because the method receives copies of the references: swapping its parameters swaps only its own copies, and the caller's variables still point at the original objects.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A swap method would need to change the caller's variables themselves — to make variable a point at what b pointed at. Java passes a copy of each reference into the parameters, so the method can swap the copies freely and the caller's variables are untouched when it returns. The same reasoning explains why a method can sort an array you pass in (mutation through the shared reference) but cannot make your variable point at a new array. To return more than one value, return an object or a record holding them.
followUps: What is the difference between mutating an object and reassigning a reference?
How would you return two values from a method?
tips: Explain it with the caller's variables, not with the word reference alone.
Contrast with sorting an array, which does work.
commonMistakes: Claiming swap fails because Java copies the object.
Expecting reassignment of a parameter to affect the caller.

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled, and they are meant for recoverable conditions such as a missing file or a failed network call, while unchecked exceptions usually signal programming errors such as a null dereference or an illegal argument. Overusing checked exceptions leaks implementation details through every caller, so many modern codebases wrap them in a meaningful unchecked exception at a boundary. Try-with-resources guarantees that each resource is closed in reverse order of opening, even when an exception occurs, and any exception thrown during close is added as a suppressed exception rather than hiding the original failure. Always close resources you open, log the original exception with context, and avoid catching Exception just to swallow it.
followUps: When would you wrap a checked exception instead of declaring it?
How do you inspect a suppressed exception?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you use a checked exception versus an unchecked exception, and how does try-with-resources change exception handling?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Checked for recoverable conditions, unchecked for programming errors; try-with-resources closes resources reliably and preserves the original exception, adding close failures as suppressed exceptions.
tips: Name a concrete recoverable case and a concrete programming-error case.
Mention suppressed exceptions — it shows you have debugged real resource code.
interviewQuestions.title: Checked vs unchecked exceptions

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: HashMap is not thread-safe and its iterators are fail-fast, so a concurrent modification during iteration usually throws ConcurrentModificationException, whereas ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and tolerate concurrent updates without throwing. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null keys and null values, because a null return from get would be ambiguous when another thread could have removed the entry. Its atomic methods such as computeIfAbsent, merge, and putIfAbsent let you update a shared map without external locking, but the mapping function must be short and side-effect free, since it may be retried. For counters or grouped results, combine it with atomic values such as LongAdder or a concurrent collection rather than synchronizing the whole map.
followUps: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values?
When is computeIfAbsent unsafe?
interviewQuestions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap differ from a synchronized HashMap, and when would you choose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap is lock-striped, thread-safe, weakly consistent for iteration, and forbids nulls; a synchronized HashMap serializes all access and still fails fast on concurrent iteration.
tips: Contrast fail-fast with weakly consistent iteration explicitly.
Warn that computeIfAbsent functions must be short and side-effect free.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronized HashMap

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool, which helps only for large, CPU-bound, splittable workloads with independent, non-blocking operations. They hurt when the source is small, the work is I/O-bound, the operations block, or the pipeline uses stateful operations such as sorted or distinct that force coordination, and they can starve other tasks sharing the common pool. Stateful lambda side effects, such as appending to a shared list, break correctness in parallel pipelines, so collect results with a proper collector instead. A good answer names the workload, checks its size, avoids blocking calls, and measures before and after rather than assuming parallelism is faster.
followUps: Why should you not do blocking I/O inside a parallel stream?
How do you collect results safely from a parallel stream?
interviewQuestions.question: When does a parallel stream help, and when does it make performance worse?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Parallel streams help only for large CPU-bound work over a splittable source; they hurt for small, blocking, or I/O-bound work and can starve the shared common pool.
tips: Give the three conditions: large, CPU-bound, splittable.
Mention that the common ForkJoinPool is shared, so a slow stream affects the whole application.
interviewQuestions.title: Parallel streams: help or harm

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: CompletableFuture chains such as thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine let you express dependent and independent async steps without blocking, while exceptionally and handle let you recover or translate failures at a defined point in the chain. The most common production failure is submitting many futures to an unbounded or too-small pool, so dependent stages queue up and the whole pipeline stalls even though no thread has deadlocked. Always supply an explicit executor for blocking or long-running stages, bound the pool and its queue, set timeouts with orTimeout, and decide where exceptions are observed, because an unobserved future failure is silently lost. For fan-out work, combine futures with allOf and then inspect each result individually rather than assuming success.
followUps: What happens when a CompletableFuture exception is never observed?
Why should blocking stages not use the common ForkJoinPool?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you chain CompletableFuture stages safely in production, and what usually goes wrong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Chain with thenApply, thenCompose, and thenCombine, handle failures explicitly, use a dedicated bounded executor for blocking stages, and apply timeouts.
tips: Name the thread-pool exhaustion failure mode, not just the API methods.
Mention orTimeout and explicit exception handling in the same answer.
interviewQuestions.title: CompletableFuture in production

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Most modern collectors divide the heap into young and old generations, because most objects die young: short-lived objects are collected cheaply in the young generation, while survivors are promoted to the old generation, which is collected less often but more expensively. G1 divides the heap into regions and targets a pause-time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first, whereas the Parallel collector prioritizes throughput and accepts longer pauses. Frequent full garbage collections, long promotion failures, or a steadily growing old generation usually point to a leak, an undersized heap, or objects that live longer than expected. Tune by measuring pause times and allocation rates first, then adjust heap size and collector choice, rather than guessing flags.
followUps: How do you tell a leak apart from a heap that is simply too small?
When would you prefer throughput over low pause time?
interviewQuestions.question: How do generational garbage collectors work, and how do you choose between G1 and Parallel GC?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Young objects are collected cheaply and survivors are promoted; G1 targets pause time with region-based collection, Parallel targets throughput with longer pauses.
tips: Explain the generational hypothesis before naming collectors.
Tie the choice to a measurable goal: pause time versus throughput.
interviewQuestions.title: Generational GC and collector choice

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Singleton is the default scope, so the container creates one instance per application context, while prototype creates a new instance on every request for the bean. The classic trap is injecting a prototype bean into a singleton: the injection happens once, so the singleton keeps the same prototype instance forever. Fix it by injecting a provider, such as ObjectProvider or Provider, and asking for a fresh instance on each use, or by using a scoped proxy. Request and session scopes only exist in a web context, and relying on them in a service layer makes the service untestable outside a request, so keep scope decisions at the edge where they belong.
followUps: How do you get a fresh prototype instance inside a singleton?
Why is request scope a poor fit for a service bean?
interviewQuestions.question: What goes wrong when a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The singleton captures one prototype instance at injection time; inject ObjectProvider or Provider and request a fresh instance per use, or use a scoped proxy.
tips: State the trap first, then the fix — interviewers want both.
Mention that prototype beans are not destroyed by the container.
interviewQuestions.title: Prototype beans in singletons

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot resolves configuration from many sources in a defined precedence order, roughly: command-line arguments and environment variables beat application properties files, which beat packaged defaults, and profile-specific files such as application-prod.properties beat the base application.properties within the same source type. Binding properties into a validated @ConfigurationProperties class is safer than scattering @Value annotations, because it groups related settings, supports relaxed binding and type conversion, and fails fast on invalid values when validation is enabled. Secrets should come from environment variables or a secret store, never from a committed properties file, and profile-specific behaviour should be expressed as configuration, not as if-statements scattered through code. When a value surprises you, check the active profiles and the effective property source order before assuming the code is wrong.
followUps: Where should secrets live, and why not in application.properties?
How do you fail fast on invalid configuration?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring Boot decide which configuration value wins, and how should you structure configuration for multiple environments?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Higher-precedence sources such as command-line arguments and environment variables beat properties files, and profile-specific files beat the base file; bind settings into validated @ConfigurationProperties classes.
tips: Recite the precedence order in one sentence.
Recommend @ConfigurationProperties over scattered @Value.
interviewQuestions.title: Profiles and configuration precedence

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A @RestControllerAdvice class centralizes exception handling across controllers, mapping each exception type to a consistent error body and HTTP status, so controllers stay focused on happy-path logic. Bean Validation annotations such as @NotNull, @Size, and @Pattern on a request DTO, triggered by @Valid, reject bad input before business logic runs, and validation failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException you can translate in the same advice class. Return ResponseEntity when the status or headers vary, such as 201 Created with a Location header after creating a resource, and keep error bodies stable with fields for a code, a message, and request context. Never leak stack traces or internal exception messages to clients, and never use exceptions for ordinary control flow.
followUps: Where does validation run relative to controller logic?
What should a stable API error body contain?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design consistent error handling and validation for a Spring MVC REST API?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Validate DTOs with Bean Validation, translate exceptions centrally in @RestControllerAdvice into stable error bodies, and use ResponseEntity when status or headers vary.
tips: Pair validation and exception translation — they belong together in the answer.
Mention 201 with a Location header as the ResponseEntity example.
interviewQuestions.title: REST error handling and validation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Derived query methods are readable for simple lookups, but they grow unwieldy for complex conditions, so use @Query for explicit JPQL or native SQL, and projections or DTO queries when you only need a few columns. Pagination with Pageable is convenient, but offset pagination degrades on large tables because the database still scans skipped rows, so keyset pagination on an ordered unique key is better for infinite-scroll or export workloads. Keep transaction boundaries at the service layer, not the repository, so a unit of work that touches several repositories commits or rolls back together, and avoid lazy-loading collections inside a controller after the transaction has closed. Count queries for Page results can also be expensive, so use Slice or a separate count only when the total is actually displayed.
followUps: When is keyset pagination better than offset pagination?
Why should transactions live at the service layer?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you choose between derived queries, @Query, and pagination strategies in Spring Data JPA?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Derived queries for simple lookups, @Query for complex or selective queries, offset pagination for small result sets, and keyset pagination for large or scrolling workloads.
tips: Name the offset-pagination cost: skipped rows are still scanned.
Put transactions at the service layer, not the repository.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA queries and pagination
