interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The attack works because browsers attach cookies automatically: a malicious page can make the victim's browser submit a form to your bank's transfer endpoint, and the session cookie goes along, so the server cannot tell the request came from the attacker. Spring Security defends this by requiring a CSRF token, a secret value rendered into your forms and checked on every state-changing request, so a request from another origin fails the check. Disabling it is safe only when the application does not rely on cookies for authentication at all, for example a stateless API using an Authorization bearer token, because then the browser has no ambient credential to abuse. For a traditional server-rendered app with session cookies, disabling CSRF leaves the application open, and the fix for a broken form is usually to include the token, not to turn the protection off.
followUps: Why does a bearer-token API not need CSRF protection?
How does the CSRF token actually stop the attack?
interviewQuestions.question: What is CSRF, and when is it safe to disable CSRF protection in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to your site, using the browser's stored session cookie. Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default; it is safe to disable only for stateless APIs, such as JWT bearer-token APIs, where no cookie authenticates the request.
tips: Explain the attack in one sentence before the defence.
Give the rule: disable only when no cookie authenticates requests.
interviewQuestions.title: CSRF protection in Spring Security

commonMistakes: Catching everything in each controller with try-catch.
Throwing generic RuntimeException, which the advice cannot distinguish.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Without central handling, every controller repeats try-catch blocks and errors come back in different shapes. A @ControllerAdvice class is a global version of a controller: methods annotated with @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) run whenever that exception escapes any controller, and they return a ResponseEntity with a status and a uniform body, for example a code, a message, and a timestamp. You can also extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler to override handling for Spring's own exceptions, such as validation failures, so they use the same error shape. The exceptions themselves should stay meaningful: throw a specific ResourceNotFoundException from the service layer instead of a generic RuntimeException, because the advice can only map what it can distinguish.
followUps: How do you make validation errors use the same error shape?
Where should the exception be thrown: controller or service?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle exceptions globally in a Spring MVC application?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a @ControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods: each method maps an exception type to a ResponseEntity with the right status and a consistent error body, so no controller needs its own try-catch.
tips: Stress the consistency win: one error shape for the whole API.
Mention ResponseEntityExceptionHandler for Spring's own exceptions.
interviewQuestions.title: Global exception handling with @ControllerAdvice

commonMistakes: Trusting the file extension for validation.
Storing uploads in a web-accessible directory.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot configures a MultipartResolver automatically, so a controller method can declare @RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file and receive the upload. The checks that matter are server-side: reject empty files, enforce a size limit, and validate the content type by inspecting the bytes rather than trusting the extension, because the extension is whatever the client claims. Store the file with a generated name in a directory outside the web root, or in object storage such as S3, and keep only the path in the database. Never save a file under its original filename in a web-accessible folder: a crafted name can overwrite other files or, if the file is executable, lead to remote code execution. The size limits live in configuration, and exceeding them produces a MaxUploadSizeExceededException, which your @ControllerAdvice should turn into a clean 413 or 400 response.
followUps: Why should you never store an upload under its original filename?
What happens when an upload exceeds the configured size limit?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle a file upload in a Spring MVC controller?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Accept a MultipartFile with @RequestParam, validate its size and type, and store it on disk or in object storage; configure limits with spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size, and never trust the client-supplied filename.
tips: Lead with the security point: never trust the filename.
Mention the size-limit exception and its handler.
interviewQuestions.title: Handling file uploads in Spring MVC

commonMistakes: Joining a table to itself without aliases.
Using an inner join and dropping employees without a manager.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A self-join is an ordinary join where both sides are the same table, distinguished by aliases: FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id. Without the aliases the query is ambiguous and the database cannot tell which copy of the table a column belongs to. The manager example is the standard one: to list each employee with their manager's name, you join the table to itself on the manager id, and a LEFT JOIN keeps employees with no manager instead of dropping them. Other uses are comparing rows, such as finding pairs of employees in the same department, and hierarchical data before recursive queries exist. The key point for the interview is that there is nothing special about the syntax: it is a normal join, and the aliases are what make it work.
followUps: How would you list employees who have no manager?
How would you find pairs of employees in the same department?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a self-join, and when would you use one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A self-join joins a table to itself using two aliases, so you can compare rows within the same table; the classic case is an employees table where each employee references a manager who is also an employee.
tips: Use the employee-manager example; it is the canonical one.
Point out that aliases are the whole trick.
interviewQuestions.title: Self-join in SQL

commonMistakes: Writing a correlated subquery that runs once per row.
Using NOT IN with nulls, which silently returns no rows.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A join is the natural tool for combining related rows: orders with their customer names, employees with their departments. A subquery is the natural tool for a question that is itself a query: employees whose salary is above the average, orders from customers who have ordered more than five times, or an EXISTS check, which stops at the first match and is often the fastest way to test existence. Correlated subqueries, which run once per outer row, are the performance trap: they look innocent and scale terribly, and rewriting one as a join is a standard optimisation. As a rule, prefer joins for combining, prefer subqueries for filtering by an aggregate or an existence test, and always check with EXPLAIN rather than guessing, because the optimiser often rewrites one form into the other anyway.
followUps: Why is a correlated subquery usually slower than a join?
When is EXISTS faster than IN?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you use a JOIN, and when is a subquery the better choice?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a JOIN when you need columns from both tables or when the relationship is the point of the query; use a subquery when you need a single value, an existence check, or a filtered set first. JOINs are usually faster, but readability decides when performance is equal.
tips: Give the rule: join to combine, subquery to filter by a computed value.
Mention EXPLAIN as the arbiter.
interviewQuestions.title: JOIN versus subquery: how to choose

commonMistakes: Using @Modifying without @Transactional.
Reading stale entities after a bulk update without clearing the context.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Derived query methods and @Query methods are reads by default; Spring Data JPA will reject an update query unless the method is annotated with @Modifying. The annotation tells Spring to call executeUpdate instead of getResultList and to return the number of affected rows. Two things are commonly forgotten. First, the transaction: a modifying query needs an active transaction, so the method needs @Transactional, or it fails at runtime. Second, staleness: entities already loaded in the persistence context are not refreshed by a bulk update, so a later read can return old values; setting clearAutomatically = true clears the context after the update, and flushAutomatically = true flushes pending changes before it. For large bulk operations, a bulk update is far cheaper than loading every entity and saving it one by one.
followUps: What goes wrong if you forget @Transactional on a @Modifying method?
Why might a read after a bulk update return stale data?
interviewQuestions.question: What is @Modifying for in Spring Data JPA, and what do people forget when they use it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Modifying marks a @Query as a write: an UPDATE or DELETE instead of a SELECT. It must run inside a transaction, so the method also needs @Transactional, and the persistence context can hold stale entities unless you clear it with clearAutomatically.
tips: Name the two forgotten pieces: the transaction and the stale context.
Mention the bulk-update cost saving.
interviewQuestions.title: @Modifying in Spring Data JPA

commonMistakes: Forgetting equals and hashCode on the key class.
Using a composite key when a surrogate id would be simpler.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Some tables are naturally identified by two columns, such as an order line identified by order id plus line number. JPA offers two mappings. With @EmbeddedId, you write one small class annotated @Embeddable that holds both fields, and the entity has a single @EmbeddedId field of that type; the key is one object, which is easy to pass around and use in queries. With @IdClass, the entity declares both key fields directly with @Id, and the id class mirrors them; this keeps the entity's fields flat but duplicates the field definitions. Whichever you choose, the key class must implement equals and hashCode correctly and be Serializable, because JPA and collections both depend on them. A practical tip: if the table has no natural composite key and you control the schema, a single surrogate id is usually simpler than a composite key.
followUps: What must a composite key class implement, and why?
When would you avoid a composite key entirely?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you map an entity whose primary key is made of two columns?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a composite key: either an @Embeddable key class held in one @EmbeddedId field, or an @IdClass that mirrors the key fields on the entity. @EmbeddedId is the cleaner and more common choice.
tips: Recommend @EmbeddedId and say why.
Mention the surrogate-key escape hatch.
interviewQuestions.title: Composite keys in JPA: @EmbeddedId versus @IdClass

commonMistakes: Applying eventual consistency to money movement.
Assuming a read immediately after a write sees the new value.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Strong consistency, the kind a single database gives you with ACID transactions, is impossible across independent services without expensive coordination, so distributed systems trade it for availability and partition tolerance. With eventual consistency, a write to one service propagates to the others through events, and readers may briefly see the old value. Whether that is fine is a business question, not a technical one: a like count that is off by one for a second is harmless, but a bank balance that is off by one is not. The design consequences are concrete: clients must tolerate stale reads, often with read-your-writes guarantees for the user who just wrote, operations must be idempotent because events can be delivered twice, and the UI should be designed so a brief inconsistency is invisible rather than alarming.
followUps: How do you give a user a read-your-writes guarantee with eventual consistency?
Why must event handlers be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.question: What is eventual consistency, and when is it acceptable?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Eventual consistency means replicas and services may disagree briefly after a write, but converge to the same value if no new writes arrive. It is acceptable when the business can tolerate a short delay, such as counts and feeds, and unacceptable when money moves, such as balances and inventory reservations.
tips: Frame it as a business decision with examples on both sides.
Mention idempotency as the practical consequence.
interviewQuestions.title: Eventual consistency in microservices

commonMistakes: Assuming a registry outage stops all traffic.
Treating a cached registry entry as permanently valid.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The registry, such as Eureka or Consul, is the phone book: services register on startup and clients look up addresses before calling. If it fails, the damage is limited by design. Clients cache the registry entries they have already fetched, so calls between already-known services continue, and Eureka's self-preservation mode deliberately stops evicting instances during a network problem rather than dropping healthy services. What breaks is change: new instances cannot be found, dead instances keep being tried until the cache refreshes, and deployments that depend on discovery stall. That is why the registry itself runs as a cluster, why clients must handle a stale entry with retries and timeouts, and why critical paths often add a fallback such as a static list or a load balancer in front of the registry.
followUps: Why do clients cache the registry, and what risk does the cache carry?
What is Eureka's self-preservation mode?
interviewQuestions.question: What happens in a microservices system if the service registry goes down?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: New services cannot register and new instances cannot be discovered, but existing services keep working because clients cache the registry locally; the registry is therefore designed for high availability, and clients fall back to their cached copy.
tips: Lead with the reassuring fact: existing traffic keeps flowing.
Name the real casualty: change and discovery of new instances.
interviewQuestions.title: What happens when the service registry fails?

commonMistakes: Forgetting that -15 starts with a minus sign.
Writing a manual loop when the question asks for streams.
followUps: How would you do it without converting to strings?
How do negative numbers change the answer?
interviewQuestions.question: Given a list of integers, find all numbers starting with 1 using Stream functions. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Convert each number to its string form, keep the ones whose first character is 1, and collect the result; the conversion is the trick, because streams have no numeric 'starts with' operation.
tips: Say why the string conversion is the trick, not the filter.
Mention the negative-number edge case.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: numbers starting with 1 using streams

commonMistakes: Saying JDK proxies work for any class.
Forgetting that final methods escape CGLIB proxies.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A JDK dynamic proxy is a runtime-generated class that implements the same interfaces as the target, so it only works when the bean implements an interface and only intercepts interface methods. A CGLIB proxy is a runtime-generated subclass of the target class, so it works with no interface, but a subclass cannot override a final method or extend a final class, so those are never advised. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB proxies, which is why injecting a bean by its concrete class usually works even when the bean implements an interface.
followUps: What happens if you inject a JDK-proxied bean by its concrete class?
Why can't a CGLIB proxy advise a final method?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Spring decide between a JDK dynamic proxy and a CGLIB proxy, and what can each one not do?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A JDK proxy implements the bean's interfaces and needs one; a CGLIB proxy subclasses the bean and works without an interface, but cannot proxy final classes or methods. Spring Boot uses CGLIB by default.
tips: Name the default first: Spring Boot uses CGLIB unless configured otherwise.
Tie the answer to a failure: a final method silently skipping advice is the classic symptom.
interviewQuestions.title: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB

commonMistakes: Claiming Spring will warn you — it does not.
Suggesting @Transactional on the calling method as a fix when the point is the called method's own boundary.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The @Transactional behaviour is an interceptor on the proxy that wraps the bean. Calls arriving from outside go through the proxy and start a transaction; a method calling another method on the same object calls this directly, bypassing the proxy entirely. The annotation is silently ignored — no error, no warning. The same applies to @Async, @Cacheable, and @PreAuthorize. Fixes: have another bean call the annotated method, inject the bean into itself through the proxy, or restructure so the caller invokes the transactional method directly.
followUps: Does @Transactional work on a private method?
How would you fix it without restructuring the classes?
interviewQuestions.question: A service method calls another @Transactional method in the same class, and no transaction starts. Why?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring applies transactions through a proxy, and a call on this never passes through the proxy, so the transactional advice never runs.
tips: Draw the proxy in words: outside call goes through it, internal call does not.
Mention that the same trap applies to @Async and @Cacheable — interviewers love the generalisation.
interviewQuestions.title: Why @Transactional fails on self-invocation

commonMistakes: Saying mappedBy owns the relationship.
Claiming both sides are written to the database.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In a bidirectional association only one side owns the foreign key. For an order and its line items, the @ManyToOne side (LineItem.order, with @JoinColumn) owns it, and the @OneToMany side declares mappedBy = "order" to say so. Hibernate writes only the owning side's state: adding a child to the parent's collection without setting child.setOrder(parent) inserts the child with a null foreign key. The standard fix is a helper method on the parent that sets both sides, so the in-memory graph and the database row cannot disagree.
followUps: What happens if you set only the inverse side?
When would you model a many-to-many with an explicit link entity?
interviewQuestions.question: What does mappedBy mean on a @OneToMany, and which side of the association owns the relationship?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: mappedBy marks the inverse side. The owning side — usually the @ManyToOne — holds the foreign key and is the only side Hibernate writes.
tips: Answer with the foreign key: whoever holds it owns the relationship.
Mention the helper-method pattern — it shows you have debugged this.
interviewQuestions.title: mappedBy and association ownership

commonMistakes: Treating the two as the same feature.
Enabling orphanRemoval on a shared association.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Cascade propagates an operation you perform: with CascadeType.REMOVE, calling remove() on the parent deletes the children too. orphanRemoval is different — it reacts to the state of the collection: removing a child from the parent's list deletes that child's row at flush time, with no explicit delete call. orphanRemoval is the right tool for privately owned children such as order line items, and the wrong tool for shared entities, where removing a reference from one parent should not delete a row other parents still use.
followUps: Would you cascade REMOVE from a parent to a shared entity?
What does CascadeType.PERSIST do?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between CascadeType.REMOVE and orphanRemoval on a @OneToMany?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Cascade REMOVE deletes children when you explicitly delete the parent; orphanRemoval deletes a child when it is removed from the parent's collection, even though the parent still exists.
tips: Contrast the trigger: an explicit operation versus a missing reference.
Give the line-item example for orphanRemoval.
interviewQuestions.title: Cascade REMOVE vs orphanRemoval

commonMistakes: Saying ReentrantLock is faster — it is not, it is more flexible.
Forgetting unlock() on the exception path.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: synchronized is the default: simple, automatically released, and understood by the JVM. ReentrantLock adds tryLock() (attempt without blocking), tryLock(timeout, unit) (give up after a wait instead of blocking forever), lockInterruptibly() (let a waiting thread be cancelled), an optional fairness policy, and multiple Condition objects per lock (for example separate not-full and not-empty conditions in a bounded buffer). The price is explicit release: every lock() must be paired with unlock() in a finally block, or an exception leaves the lock held forever.
followUps: What does a Condition give you that wait/notify does not?
Why is fairness usually left off?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose ReentrantLock over synchronized?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: When you need a timeout, an interruptible wait, fairness, or multiple Conditions — none of which synchronized offers.
tips: List the four features, then name the cost: manual unlock in finally.
Give the bounded-buffer example for multiple Conditions.
interviewQuestions.title: ReentrantLock vs synchronized

commonMistakes: Saying virtual threads are faster — they make blocking cheap, not computation fast.
Forgetting that synchronized is the pinning cause.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A platform thread maps one-to-one to an operating system thread and occupies it while blocked. A virtual thread runs on a carrier thread from a small pool; when it blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it and the carrier runs another virtual thread, so a million virtual threads can be alive at once. Pinning breaks that: blocking while holding a monitor (synchronized) or inside a native call keeps the virtual thread mounted, so the carrier cannot do other work and the pool can starve under load. The fix is to use ReentrantLock, which does not pin, and to keep blocking calls out of synchronized blocks.
followUps: Why should you not pool virtual threads?
Does a virtual thread help CPU-bound work?
interviewQuestions.question: How does a virtual thread differ from a platform thread, and what is pinning?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A virtual thread is JVM-managed and cheap to block: it unmounts from its carrier platform thread while waiting. Pinning is when it cannot unmount — blocking inside synchronized or a native call — so the carrier stays occupied.
tips: Explain mount and unmount before naming pinning.
Give the ReentrantLock remedy, not just the problem.
interviewQuestions.title: Virtual threads, carriers, and pinning

commonMistakes: Claiming virtual threads make everything faster.
Creating unbounded virtual threads against a 20-connection pool.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Virtual threads help when threads block on I/O: the cost they remove is the cost of a blocked thread. A computation that never blocks gains nothing and pays scheduling overhead, so CPU-bound work belongs on a bounded platform-thread pool. A small, fixed number of tasks is simpler on a platform pool too. And a million concurrent requests still hit one database: without a limit such as a semaphore or a bounded connection pool, virtual threads can overwhelm a downstream service faster than a bounded pool would. They also multiply ThreadLocal state — a million virtual threads can mean a million copies of a ThreadLocal value.
followUps: What executor would you use for virtual threads?
How do you bound concurrency to a database with virtual threads?
interviewQuestions.question: When should you not use virtual threads?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: For CPU-bound work, for a small fixed set of long-lived tasks, or when the downstream system cannot handle unbounded concurrency — virtual threads remove the thread bottleneck, not the resource bottleneck.
tips: Name the bottleneck virtual threads do not remove.
Mention ThreadLocal as the less obvious hazard.
interviewQuestions.title: When not to use virtual threads

commonMistakes: Saying the index is hash % capacity.
Saying spreading is done to make hashes random.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A key's bucket index is (n - 1) & hash, where n is the table length. Because capacity is always a power of two, n - 1 is a run of 1-bits, so this is equivalent to hash % n but costs a bitwise AND instead of a division. The catch is that only the low bits of the hash decide the bucket — so HashMap first spreads the hash by XOR-ing it with its own top 16 bits, mixing the high bits into the low ones. Without spreading, keys whose hash codes differ only in the high bits would all collide in the same bucket.
followUps: Why must capacity stay a power of two?
What is the default load factor, and when does the table resize?
interviewQuestions.question: Why does HashMap spread the hash code, and how is the bucket index computed?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The index uses only the low bits of the hash, so spreading XORs the high bits down ((h ^ (h >>> 16))). The index is (n - 1) & hash, which works because capacity is always a power of two.
tips: Write the two formulas: the spread and (n - 1) & hash.
Explain why the power-of-two capacity matters for the AND trick.
interviewQuestions.title: HashMap hash spreading and indexing

commonMistakes: Saying ConcurrentHashMap locks the whole map.
Storing null and expecting it to work like HashMap.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In concurrent code, map.get(key) returning null must mean one thing: the key is absent. If null values were allowed, a null result could mean absent or present-with-null, and no atomic check could distinguish them. For safety, ConcurrentHashMap inserts into an empty bin with a compare-and-swap (no lock), synchronizes on the first node of an occupied bin so only writers to that bucket contend, lets multiple threads cooperate on a resize, and counts size with counter cells instead of one contended counter. Iterators are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException and may or may not show concurrent updates.
followUps: How would you atomically increment a counter in a ConcurrentHashMap?
When would you still use Collections.synchronizedMap?
interviewQuestions.question: Why does ConcurrentHashMap forbid null keys and values, and how does it stay thread-safe without one big lock?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Null is forbidden so that get() returning null unambiguously means absent. Safety comes from CAS on empty bins and synchronizing on the first node of an occupied bin — reads never block.
tips: Answer the null question first — it is about ambiguity, not convenience.
Contrast bin-level locking with the old whole-map lock.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap nulls and locking

commonMistakes: Describing the implicit flow as the current standard.
Confusing the code with the token.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The client redirects the user to the authorization server with the requested scopes and a code_challenge (a hash of a random code_verifier). The user authenticates and consents, and the server redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The client exchanges the code for tokens, sending the original code_verifier; the server checks it against the challenge. Even if the code leaks from the redirect, nobody else can redeem it, because they do not have the verifier. PKCE is required for public clients such as mobile and single-page apps, which cannot keep a secret, and recommended for every client. The older implicit flow, which returned tokens in the redirect itself, is deprecated.
followUps: What is the difference between an access token and an id_token?
Why is the implicit flow deprecated?
interviewQuestions.question: Walk through the authorization code flow with PKCE. What does the code verifier prove?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The client creates a random verifier, sends its hash as the challenge, and presents the verifier when exchanging the code for tokens — proving the exchange comes from the client that started the flow.
tips: Walk the four steps in order: challenge, consent, code, exchange.
Say what the verifier proves — same client, not just any client.
interviewQuestions.title: Authorization code flow with PKCE

commonMistakes: Saying primitives always live on the stack.
Saying objects always live on the heap with no exception.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The stack holds method frames: local variables (primitive locals and reference variables) and return addresses, freed when the method returns. Objects live on the heap — including their fields, so an int field of an object lives on the heap inside that object, and an int array's elements live on the heap in the array. The JIT compiler can also invert the rule through escape analysis: an object that never escapes its method may be allocated on the stack instead of the heap. The right mental model is about lifetimes, not types: stack data dies with the method call, heap data lives until unreachable.
followUps: Where does a local reference variable live, and where does its object live?
What is escape analysis?
interviewQuestions.question: Do primitives always live on the stack?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: No. Primitive locals live in stack frames, but primitive fields live on the heap as part of their object — and escape analysis can stack-allocate objects too.
tips: Answer with locals versus fields, not with primitives versus objects.
Mention escape analysis as the exception that proves the rule.
interviewQuestions.title: Do primitives always live on the stack?

commonMistakes: Saying the two cost the same.
Assuming PostgreSQL tables are clustered like InnoDB's.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A clustered index decides the physical order of the table's rows — the table itself is stored in index order, and a table has at most one, usually its primary key (InnoDB stores tables clustered by primary key). A non-clustered (secondary) index maps indexed values to row locations in a separate structure, and the database follows the pointer to fetch the row. A range scan on the clustered key is cheap because the rows are adjacent; a lookup through a secondary index costs a pointer chase per row, and a secondary index returning a large fraction of the table can be slower than a full scan, because random fetches cost more than a sequential read.
followUps: What is a covering index, and why does it avoid the extra hop?
Why can a table have only one clustered index?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A clustered index stores the table's rows in index order (one per table, usually the primary key); a non-clustered index is a separate structure that points at rows, so each lookup costs an extra hop.
tips: Lead with physical order versus pointer.
Mention InnoDB's primary-key clustering as the concrete case.
interviewQuestions.title: Clustered vs non-clustered indexes

commonMistakes: Retrying a poison message forever with no dead-letter topic.
Assuming the dead-letter topic is monitored just because it exists.
Committing offsets before processing so failures vanish silently.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A @KafkaListener that throws has its record redelivered, because offsets are committed only after successful processing. Without a failure policy, a poison message — one that fails on every attempt — is retried forever and blocks its whole partition. The standard shape is a DefaultErrorHandler (the current name in Spring Kafka 3.x) with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and a FixedBackOff: after the configured retries, the recoverer publishes the failed record to a dead-letter topic, by default the original topic name plus -dlt, preserving the original headers including the exception, and the container commits the offset. The dead-letter topic must be watched — an alert or dashboard — or it becomes a quieter form of data loss. The listener itself must still be idempotent, because retries before the dead-letter step can run the same record twice.
followUps: Where do dead-lettered records go, and how would you replay one?
Why must the listener still be idempotent even with a dead-letter topic?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you stop one failing Kafka record from blocking its partition in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Configure a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer on the listener container factory: retry the record with a backoff, then publish it to a dead-letter topic and commit the offset so the consumer moves on.
tips: Name the two classes: DefaultErrorHandler and DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer.
Mention that the DLT needs monitoring, not just existence.
interviewQuestions.title: Kafka listeners: retries and dead-letter topics

commonMistakes: Using condition where unless is needed, and wondering why #result is unavailable.
Caching nulls for missing rows with no TTL.
Assuming sync=true works across multiple caches.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: condition and unless both take SpEL, but at opposite moments. condition runs before the method, so it decides whether caching applies at all — condition = "#id > 0" skips the cache entirely for invalid ids — and it cannot see #result because the method has not run. unless runs after the method, so it judges the computed value — unless = "#result == null" keeps a missing row out of the cache, so a record created later is found immediately instead of serving a cached null until TTL expires. sync=true addresses the stampede: when a hot key expires, concurrent misses for that key block on the first caller, which loads once and shares the value. It works for a single cache only, and it relies on the cache implementation supporting the blocking load, which Spring Data Redis's RedisCache does.
followUps: Why would you cache a null for a missing row at all, and with what TTL?
What happens if you put sync=true on an annotation with several caches?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between condition and unless on @Cacheable, and what does sync=true do?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: condition is evaluated before the method runs and can only use the arguments; unless is evaluated after and can also use #result. sync=true makes concurrent misses for the same key wait on the first loader instead of all hitting the database.
tips: Anchor on the evaluation moment: condition before, unless after.
Mention that unless is the only one that can see #result.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Cache: condition vs unless, and sync=true

commonMistakes: Returning a ProblemDetail and expecting Spring to fill in instance automatically — a custom handler must set it.
Inventing a custom error envelope when the standard exists.
Enabling the property and assuming business exceptions are covered too.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: RFC 9457 defines one standard JSON shape for API errors instead of every team inventing its own envelope: type (a URI for the problem kind, default about:blank), title (a short summary, same for every occurrence), status, detail (this occurrence, for humans), and instance (this occurrence's URI, usually the request path), plus extension members such as a stable error code added with setProperty. Spring's ProblemDetail models it, and returning one from an @ExceptionHandler sets the response status from its status field and the content type to application/problem+json. For Spring MVC's own exceptions — 404 for an unknown URL, 405, 415 — spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true makes Boot return them in the same shape; it is off by default because it changes every default error body. The fuller version is an advice extending ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, whose methods already return ProblemDetail for each framework exception. ProblemDetail standardizes the body; @RestControllerAdvice still decides which exception maps to which problem.
followUps: What does spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true change, and why is it off by default?
How do you keep a stable machine-readable error code inside a ProblemDetail?
interviewQuestions.question: What is ProblemDetail, and how does it relate to RFC 9457?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ProblemDetail is Spring Framework 6's implementation of RFC 9457 (which supersedes RFC 7807): a standard error body with type, title, status, detail, and instance, served as application/problem+json. Returning one from an @ExceptionHandler sets the status and content type from the object.
tips: Name the five members and the media type.
Note that RFC 9457 supersedes RFC 7807 — interviewers check for the current number.
interviewQuestions.title: ProblemDetail and RFC 9457 error responses

commonMistakes: Implementing Cloneable and forgetting to deep-copy mutable fields.
Assuming clone() runs a constructor.
Overriding finalize() to clean up instead of using close() and Cleaner.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Object.clone() copies field by field: primitives by value, references by reference. That is a shallow copy — the clone and the original share every mutable object they point to, so mutating a list through one mutates it for the other. A deep copy duplicates the mutable parts as well, so the two are independent. clone() is awkward to use correctly: the class must implement Cloneable, a marker interface that declares no clone() method, or clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime even though the code compiled; the override must be public, call super.clone(), and then deep-copy each mutable field by hand; and clone() bypasses constructors, so constructor invariants are not checked on a clone. Cloning an array is shallow too. A copy constructor — new Team(other) — avoids all of it: no interface, no checked exception, the normal constructor path runs, and it works with final fields. That is why Effective Java calls Cloneable broken and prefers copy constructors.
followUps: If a class holds a mutable list, what does a correct clone() have to do?
Why does cloning an array not give you a deep copy?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy, and why is clone() risky?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the fields, so mutable referenced objects are shared; a deep copy duplicates the mutable parts too. clone() is shallow by default, needs the marker interface Cloneable, bypasses constructors, and throws CloneNotSupportedException at runtime — a copy constructor is usually the safer choice.
tips: Trace a concrete example: two objects sharing one list.
Quote the Effective Java verdict and say what it refers to.
interviewQuestions.title: clone(): shallow vs deep copy, and copy constructors

commonMistakes: Assuming the close exception replaces the body exception.
Printing only getMessage() and never checking getSuppressed().
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Two exceptions can occur: one from the try body and one from closing a resource. Try-with-resources keeps the body's exception as the primary one and attaches the close exception with addSuppressed, so getSuppressed() returns it instead of it being lost. If the body completes normally and only the close throws, the close exception becomes the primary one. addSuppressed is also available to your own code when combining failures, for example when a cleanup step fails while another exception is already in flight. The point for an interview is the ordering rule: the body wins, the close is suppressed, nothing is silently dropped.
followUps: How do you read the suppressed exceptions from a caught exception?
What happens if the body succeeds but the close throws?
interviewQuestions.question: What happens to an exception thrown while a try-with-resources resource is closing?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It is attached to the primary exception as a suppressed exception, retrievable with getSuppressed() — it is not lost, and it never replaces the exception thrown by the try body.
tips: State the ordering rule first: body wins, close is suppressed.
interviewQuestions.title: Suppressed exceptions in try-with-resources

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: PECS summarizes wildcard use: use extends when you only produce values from a structure, and super when you only consume values into it, because a List of Number cannot accept a List of Integer as a subtype even though Integer is a subtype of Number. Type erasure means generic type arguments are removed at compile time, so a List of String and a List of Integer are the same class at runtime, you cannot overload methods that differ only by generic argument, and you cannot create arrays of a parameterized type directly. The compiler inserts casts and bridge methods so overriding still works after erasure, which is why reflection sometimes reveals synthetic bridge methods. When erasure loses information you need at runtime, pass an explicit Class token or a type token instead of fighting the type system.
followUps: Why can you not overload a method on List of String versus List of Integer?
How do you recover type information lost to erasure?
interviewQuestions.question: Explain PECS and type erasure, and the practical limits they place on generic code.
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: PECS: extends for producers, super for consumers; erasure removes type arguments at runtime, so generic overloads and parameterized arrays are impossible and reflection may show bridge methods.
tips: Give one producer example and one consumer example.
Mention bridge methods — senior interviewers listen for them.
interviewQuestions.title: Generics: PECS and erasure

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: ConcurrentHashMap scales by striping locks across bins rather than locking the whole map, and its atomic bulk methods such as compute, merge, and forEach operate per bin, so they do not give you a consistent snapshot across the whole map. A mapping function in computeIfAbsent must be short, non-blocking, and side-effect free, because it can run while holding a bin lock and may be invoked more than once under contention, which can stall other threads or cause surprising duplicate work. Sizing matters less than in HashMap because concurrency level is a hint, not a hard segment count, but an undersized map still resizes under load, and a huge initial capacity wastes memory. For high-contention counters, prefer LongAdder over AtomicLong inside the map, and for compound multi-key updates, accept that you need an external lock or a redesign, not a single atomic map call.
followUps: Why is there no atomic operation across two keys?
When does LongAdder beat AtomicLong?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the scaling limits and traps of ConcurrentHashMap in high-contention code?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It scales by bin-level locking, but compute functions run under a bin lock and may repeat, bulk operations are not whole-map atomic, and multi-key updates need external coordination.
tips: Name the computeIfAbsent trap specifically.
State plainly that no map call is atomic across two keys.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentHashMap at scale

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A correct parallel reduction needs an associative, stateless combiner and an identity that is truly neutral, otherwise results vary between runs depending on how work is split. Stateful intermediate operations such as sorted, distinct, and limit on an unordered stream force buffering or coordination that can erase parallel gains, and encounter order adds further coordination costs that an unordered stream avoids. Short-circuiting operations such as findAny are faster in parallel than findFirst, which must respect order. Before parallelizing, check that the source splits efficiently — a LinkedList or an iterator-based stream splits poorly — that the per-element work is large enough to outweigh splitting overhead, and that no operation blocks or mutates shared state.
followUps: Why does a parallel reduce give different answers if the combiner is not associative?
Why is findAny faster than findFirst in parallel?
interviewQuestions.question: What makes a stream reduction correct in parallel, and which operations destroy parallel performance?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Parallel reduction needs an associative combiner and a true identity; stateful operations, encounter order, poor splitting, and blocking or mutating operations destroy its gains.
tips: Use associativity as the correctness test.
Mention findAny versus findFirst as the concrete ordering example.
interviewQuestions.title: Parallel stream correctness

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An executor saturates in stages: tasks queue up, threads grow to the maximum, the queue fills, and then the rejection policy decides whether callers block, run the task themselves, or drop it — and the default abort policy throws RejectedExecutionException at the worst moment. A bounded queue with caller-runs or a backpressure-aware policy protects downstream systems, while an unbounded queue hides overload until memory or latency explodes. Separate executors by workload class — CPU-bound, blocking I/O, and scheduled work — so one slow dependency cannot starve everything else, and expose queue depth, active threads, and rejections as metrics with alerts. Virtual threads change the calculus for blocking I/O by making a thread per task cheap, but they do not remove the need for bounds, timeouts, and backpressure when the downstream system itself is the bottleneck.
followUps: Why is an unbounded queue more dangerous than a rejection?
When do virtual threads not solve saturation?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you design an executor so overload degrades gracefully instead of crashing the service?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Bound the queue, choose an explicit rejection policy, separate executors by workload, and alert on queue depth and rejections; virtual threads help blocking I/O but do not remove downstream limits.
tips: Walk through the saturation stages in order.
Warn that an unbounded queue hides overload until it is too late.
interviewQuestions.title: Executor saturation and backpressure

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start from the symptom: long pauses point to garbage collection logs and heap sizing, a steadily growing heap points to a leak, and high CPU without progress points to a hot loop or lock contention. Enable GC logging, then read pause times, allocation rate, and promotion rate before touching flags, and take a heap dump only after confirming the heap is actually growing, since a dump freezes or slows the process. Analyze the dump for the largest retained objects and their shortest paths to GC roots, which usually reveal a static cache, a listener never deregistered, or an unbounded collection. Metaspace growth points instead to classloader leaks, often from repeated redeploys, while native memory growth points outside the heap entirely. Fix the retention cause, then tune the collector; tuning flags around a leak only postpones the outage.
followUps: How do you distinguish a leak from a heap that is too small?
What does growth in Metaspace, rather than the heap, suggest?
interviewQuestions.question: Production heap usage climbs until the service restarts. How do you diagnose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Confirm growth with GC logs, identify whether it is heap, Metaspace, or native memory, then analyze a heap dump for dominant retained objects and their paths to GC roots and fix the retention cause.
tips: Order the answer: confirm, locate, analyze, fix — not flags first.
Name the usual suspects: static caches, unremoved listeners, unbounded collections.
interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing a production memory leak

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring AOP and @Transactional work through proxies: a call from outside the bean goes through the proxy, which starts a transaction or applies advice, while a call from one method of the bean to another bypasses the proxy entirely, so the annotation on the called method is silently ignored. The same applies to private methods, which proxies cannot intercept, and to final classes or methods with JDK dynamic proxies. The fixes are to restructure so the transactional method is called through another bean, to self-inject the proxy, or to use AspectJ weaving when proxy limits are truly unacceptable. This also explains why @Transactional on a method that only calls another method in the same class appears to do nothing, and why a rollback only happens for unchecked exceptions by default unless rollbackFor is configured.
followUps: Why does @Transactional not work on a private method?
How do you make a self-call go through the proxy?
interviewQuestions.question: Why does @Transactional sometimes silently do nothing, and how do proxies explain it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Proxies only intercept external calls, so self-invocation and private methods bypass @Transactional; call through another bean or the proxy, and remember rollback is unchecked-only by default.
tips: Explain the proxy mechanism before the fix.
Mention rollbackFor, since it is the second half of the same interview question.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring proxies and self-invocation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Auto-configuration classes are ordered and conditional, so when two starters provide the same bean, the one whose conditions match and that is ordered first wins, and a user-defined bean of the same type normally makes auto-configuration back off via @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Conflicts usually come from an explicit @Bean that shadows the auto-configured one, a starter pulled in transitively that you did not expect, or a condition such as @ConditionalOnClass that behaves differently in tests versus production because the classpath differs. Debug with the auto-configuration report, which lists what applied, what was excluded, and why each candidate was skipped, and with the conditions evaluation report in tests. Prefer excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining a replacement bean deliberately over broad component-scan exclusions, which hide future surprises.
followUps: How do you find which starter brought in an unwanted bean?
When is excluding an auto-configuration better than overriding its bean?
interviewQuestions.question: Two starters configure the same bean and the wrong one wins. How do you diagnose and resolve it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Check conditions, ordering, and the auto-configuration report; a user bean normally backs auto-configuration off, so resolve conflicts by excluding a specific auto-configuration or defining the intended bean explicitly.
tips: Name the auto-configuration report as the first diagnostic step.
Distinguish transitive starter surprises from deliberate overrides.
interviewQuestions.title: Auto-configuration conflicts

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Filters run at the servlet level, before Spring MVC dispatches, so they see every request but not the handler, while interceptors run inside Spring MVC around the handler, with access to the controller method and model, and argument resolvers and exception resolvers run even closer to the handler. Use filters for cross-cutting transport concerns such as logging and authentication headers, interceptors for handler-aware concerns such as feature flags or tenant context, and @ControllerAdvice for consistent error translation. For asynchronous handling, Callable and DeferredResult release the request thread while work completes, and WebFlux-style reactive endpoints only help when the whole downstream chain is non-blocking; wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type just moves the blockage. Idempotency for retried POSTs belongs at the API layer with an idempotency key stored with the result, not in the client retry logic alone.
followUps: Why can a filter not know which controller will handle a request?
When does async handling not improve throughput?
interviewQuestions.question: How do filters, interceptors, and async handling differ in Spring MVC, and where does idempotency belong?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Filters run before dispatch without handler knowledge, interceptors run around the handler, async releases the request thread, and idempotency belongs server-side with a stored key and result.
tips: Order the layers from outermost to innermost.
Flag wrapping a blocking call in a reactive type as fake async.
interviewQuestions.title: Filters, interceptors, and async MVC

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Optimistic locking with a @Version column lets concurrent updates proceed and fails the loser with an OptimisticLockException instead of silently overwriting, which suits low-contention data such as user profiles, while pessimistic locking suits high-contention resources such as inventory counts. Isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency: read committed prevents dirty reads, repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads, and serializable prevents phantoms, but each stronger level costs throughput and increases lock waits. Lost updates, phantom reads, and write skew are the anomalies to name, and the fix is usually a version column plus a retry for the loser, or a pessimistic lock for the contested row, rather than raising the global isolation level. Second-level caching helps read-heavy reference data but can serve stale entities across nodes, so it needs explicit invalidation and must never cache frequently mutated data.
followUps: When would you choose pessimistic over optimistic locking?
Why is raising the global isolation level usually the wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle concurrent updates in JPA, and what do isolation levels actually buy you?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Optimistic locking with @Version for low contention, pessimistic locks for hot rows, and isolation levels chosen per anomaly, not raised globally; cache only stable reference data.
tips: Pair each locking strategy with its contention profile.
Name one anomaly per isolation level instead of reciting definitions.
interviewQuestions.title: JPA locking and isolation

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Two-phase commit gives strong consistency across services but couples them to a coordinator and blocks on coordinator failure, so most systems accept eventual consistency and design for it. A saga sequences local transactions with compensating actions for rollback, but compensations are not true rollbacks: they are new business operations that must themselves be idempotent and must handle partial failure. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem by writing the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, then relaying it asynchronously, so an event is never lost and never sent without its state change. Consumers must still be idempotent, because at-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal, and event schemas must evolve compatibly so old consumers keep working.
followUps: Why is a compensating action not the same as a rollback?
How does the outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you keep data consistent across microservices without distributed transactions?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use sagas with idempotent compensations for multi-service workflows and the transactional outbox for reliable event publication, and make every consumer idempotent under at-least-once delivery.
tips: Contrast 2PC blocking with saga compensation explicitly.
Name the dual-write problem — it is the heart of the question.
interviewQuestions.title: Sagas and the transactional outbox

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and running totals compute over a window of rows without collapsing them, so you can rank orders per customer or compute a moving average while keeping every row. Offset pagination with LIMIT and OFFSET is simple but scans and discards skipped rows, so it slows as the offset grows and can skip or repeat rows when data changes between pages. Keyset pagination, filtering on an ordered unique key such as a timestamp plus id, stays fast at any depth and is stable under inserts, but it cannot jump to an arbitrary page number. Covering indexes, which include every column a query needs, let the database answer from the index alone, but each extra index costs write performance and storage, so verify with the execution plan and measure on realistic data volumes.
followUps: Why can offset pagination skip rows when data changes?
When is a covering index worth its write cost?
interviewQuestions.question: When do window functions and keyset pagination beat GROUP BY and OFFSET pagination?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Window functions rank and aggregate without collapsing rows; keyset pagination on an ordered unique key stays fast and stable at depth, while OFFSET scans skipped rows and shifts under concurrent writes.
tips: Give one window-function example and one keyset example.
State the OFFSET weakness in terms of scanning, not just slowness.
interviewQuestions.title: Window functions and keyset pagination

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The task is to design an LRU cache with get and put in constant time. The idiomatic approach pairs a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency: the map gives constant-time lookup, and the list lets you move a node to the front on access and evict the tail node on overflow, both in constant time. On get, return the value and move its node to the front; on put, insert or update the node, move it to the front, and if the size exceeds capacity, remove the tail node from both the list and the map. A linked hash map in access-order mode provides this out of the box in Java, but interviewers usually want the map-plus-list structure explained, and for a concurrent version you must add locking or sharding rather than assuming the structure is thread-safe.
followUps: How would you make this cache thread-safe?
How does the design change if eviction must consider entry size, not just count?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: design an LRU cache with constant-time get and put. What data structures do you combine, and why?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Combine a hash map for constant-time lookup with a doubly linked list for recency order: move accessed nodes to the front and evict from the tail.
tips: Explain why each structure alone is insufficient.
Mention LinkedHashMap access-order mode, then explain the underlying structure anyway.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: LRU cache design

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: First, establish whether threads are blocked, deadlocked, or merely busy: thread dumps taken a few seconds apart show threads stuck in the same place for a deadlock or lock wait, versus threads moving through different code for CPU saturation. A common root cause is a thread pool exhausted by calls to a slow downstream service without timeouts, so every request thread waits and new requests queue until the service appears dead. Mitigate immediately by shedding load or restarting with bounded pools and timeouts, then fix the dependency contract: add timeouts, bulkheads per dependency, and circuit breakers, and alert on queue depth before it reaches saturation. A post-incident review should ask why the missing timeout was not caught by a checklist or test, because the same failure will recur with the next slow dependency.
followUps: How do thread dumps distinguish deadlock from CPU saturation?
What metric would have warned you before saturation?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: a service stops responding under normal traffic, CPU is low, and restarts only help briefly. How do you diagnose it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Low CPU plus unresponsiveness suggests thread-pool exhaustion or deadlock; compare thread dumps over time, then bound pools, add timeouts and bulkheads, and alert on queue depth.
tips: Use the low-CPU clue — it rules out a hot loop.
Name bulkheads as the structural fix, not just timeouts.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: thread-pool exhaustion

interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Records give concise immutable data carriers with automatically generated equals, hashCode, and accessors, and they suit DTOs and value objects, but they are final and cannot extend another class, so they are a poor fit for entities with evolving behaviour or frameworks that require proxies and no-arg construction. Sealed classes restrict which classes may extend them, which makes a hierarchy exhaustive and lets pattern-matching switches be checked by the compiler, and pattern matching replaces chains of instanceof checks and casts with a single readable form. Virtual threads make a thread-per-request style cheap for blocking I/O workloads, but they do not help CPU-bound work and they can pin a carrier thread when code synchronizes on a monitor. Migrate incrementally: introduce records and pattern matching where they clarify code, and adopt virtual threads only after confirming the workload is blocking I/O and the libraries used do not pin carriers.
followUps: Why are records a poor fit for JPA entities?
When does a virtual thread pin its carrier thread?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide where records, sealed classes, pattern matching, and virtual threads actually help?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Records for immutable data carriers, sealed classes for exhaustive hierarchies, pattern matching for type dispatch, and virtual threads only for blocking I/O workloads that do not pin carriers.
tips: Give one good fit and one poor fit per feature.
Warn about carrier pinning for virtual threads — it is the current senior-level trap.
interviewQuestions.title: Modern Java: where each feature fits

commonMistakes: Storing listeners in a strong collection and leaking the objects they point to.
Expecting get() on a phantom reference to return the object.
Using soft references as a substitute for a bounded cache with an eviction policy.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A strong reference is an ordinary variable: as long as it exists, the object cannot be collected. A soft reference (SoftReference) is cleared only when the JVM is running low on memory, which makes it a reasonable fit for a memory-sensitive cache that you are happy to rebuild. A weak reference (WeakReference) does not stop collection at all: the object is reclaimed at the next collection once only weak references remain, which is why WeakHashMap is used for listener registries and metadata that must not keep the key alive. A phantom reference (PhantomReference) never lets you reach the object through get(), which always returns null; it exists only so a ReferenceQueue can tell you the object has been reclaimed, which is the safe way to run cleanup after finalization was removed. The common mistake is using a strong reference inside a cache or listener list and then wondering why the heap grows: the objects are reachable, so no collector will ever free them.
followUps: Why is WeakHashMap a natural fit for listener registries?
How would you build a cache that the collector may empty under memory pressure?
Why was finalization replaced by phantom references and cleaners?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the four reference types in Java, and how does each one affect when the garbage collector can reclaim an object?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strong references keep an object alive; soft references are cleared only when memory is short, weak references are cleared at the next collection, and phantom references only let you know an object has been reclaimed.
tips: Order them by strength: strong, soft, weak, phantom.
Give one real use for each instead of reciting definitions.
interviewQuestions.title: Strong, soft, weak, and phantom references

commonMistakes: Treating Metaspace growth as a heap leak and tuning heap flags.
Leaving Metaspace uncapped in production.
Forgetting that JDBC drivers and shutdown hooks can pin a classloader.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Before Java 8, class metadata lived in PermGen, a fixed-size part of the heap that threw OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space when an application loaded too many classes, which happened often with repeated redeploys. Java 8 moved that metadata to Metaspace, which lives in native memory outside the heap and by default grows until the operating system runs out of memory, although you can cap it with MaxMetaspaceSize. The practical difference for diagnosis is that a growing heap points to retained objects, while a growing Metaspace points to classes being loaded and never unloaded, usually because a classloader is held by a static reference, a thread-local, or a registered driver or listener. Setting a cap is worth doing in production: without one, a classloader leak consumes native memory until the whole process is killed, and with one, it fails fast with a clear Metaspace error instead.
followUps: Why can a class only be unloaded when its classloader is unreachable?
What is a sensible MaxMetaspaceSize for a service, and why set one at all?
How do repeated redeploys in the same JVM cause Metaspace growth?
interviewQuestions.question: What is Metaspace, how does it differ from PermGen, and what does Metaspace growth tell you in production?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8 and holds class metadata in native memory with a default limit that grows as needed, so steady Metaspace growth usually points to a classloader leak rather than a heap leak.
tips: Contrast the failure mode: PermGen failed fast, Metaspace grows silently.
Tie the diagnosis to classloaders, not to heap dumps.
interviewQuestions.title: Metaspace versus PermGen

commonMistakes: Reading fields in a different order than they were written.
Forgetting the public no-arg constructor and getting an InvalidClassException.
Using Externalizable when plain Serializable with transient fields would do.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: With Serializable, the JVM uses reflection to write the object's fields for you, which is easy but gives you no say over the format, the size, or which fields are included beyond marking fields transient. Externalizable extends Serializable and requires a public no-arg constructor plus readExternal and writeExternal methods that you write yourself, so you decide the exact bytes, the order, and how to handle fields added in a later version. That control is useful when the default format is too large, when you need a stable wire format across versions, or when some fields need custom handling such as encryption. The price is that you must keep the read and write order in step yourself, and forgetting a field or reading in the wrong order corrupts the stream silently. For most application code, Serializable plus a serialVersionUID and a few transient fields is enough; reach for Externalizable when the serialized form itself is part of your contract.
followUps: Why does Externalizable require a public no-arg constructor?
What goes wrong if readExternal reads fields in a different order than writeExternal wrote them?
How would you keep a serialized form compatible when you add a field?
interviewQuestions.question: How does Externalizable differ from Serializable, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Serializable lets the JVM write every non-transient field automatically; Externalizable hands full control to your readExternal and writeExternal methods, so you choose exactly what is written and in what order.
tips: Frame it as control versus convenience.
Mention the no-arg constructor requirement; interviewers listen for it.
interviewQuestions.title: Externalizable versus Serializable

commonMistakes: Assuming loadClass runs static initialisers.
Breaking parent delegation and loading two copies of the same class.
Keeping a reference to a classloader and wondering why its classes never unload.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A JVM has three built-in loaders in a parent chain: the bootstrap loader loads the core JDK classes, the platform loader loads platform modules, and the application loader loads classes from the classpath. A custom loader, such as the one a web container creates per application, sits below these. Loading follows parent delegation: a loader asks its parent first and only loads the class itself if no parent can, which is what stops an application from replacing a core class like java.lang.String with its own version. Class.forName() loads the class and runs its static initialisers immediately, which is why it is used to trigger driver registration; ClassLoader.loadClass() only loads and links the class, and its static block runs later when the class is first used. That difference matters when a static block has side effects or when you want to inspect a class without running its initialisation. Classes are only unloaded when their loader becomes unreachable, which is why a leaked loader keeps every class it loaded alive in Metaspace.
followUps: Why does parent delegation stop an application replacing java.lang.String?
When would you create a custom classloader, and what breaks if you skip delegation?
Why does a leaked classloader show up as Metaspace growth?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the classloaders in a JVM, how does delegation work, and how do Class.forName() and ClassLoader.loadClass() differ?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Bootstrap, platform, and application loaders delegate upwards before loading a class themselves; forName loads and initialises the class, while loadClass only loads it and leaves static initialisation for later.
tips: Draw the three loaders as a chain before explaining delegation.
State the forName versus loadClass difference as initialise now versus initialise later.
interviewQuestions.title: Classloaders: types, delegation, and loading a class

commonMistakes: Returning a shallow copy and letting callers mutate shared state.
Forgetting to make clone public or to handle CloneNotSupportedException.
Deep-copying immutable fields such as Strings for no benefit.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A shallow copy creates a new object and copies each field value across, so a field that points to a list or another object still points to the same list or object in both copies; changing it through one copy changes it for the other. A deep copy also copies every referenced object, so the two graphs are fully independent, which is what you want when the copy must be safe to mutate on its own. Java's built-in route is awkward: Cloneable is only a marker interface, Object.clone() is protected and throws CloneNotSupportedException, and the default implementation is shallow, so you must override clone, make it public, handle the exception, and manually deep-copy each mutable field yourself. For that reason, most teams prefer a copy constructor or a small factory method that builds a new object field by field: the intent is visible, the depth is explicit, and there is no checked exception or protected method to work around. Whichever route you take, document whether the copy is deep or shallow, because callers will assume one or the other.
followUps: When is a shallow copy actually safe to hand out?
How would you deep-copy an object graph without writing clone at all?
Why do many teams avoid Cloneable in favour of a copy constructor?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between deep and shallow cloning, and what are the traps in Java's Cloneable design?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares its referenced fields; a deep copy duplicates those fields too. Cloneable is a marker interface with a protected, exception-throwing clone method, so it is easy to get wrong.
tips: Give one shared-reference example that shows the shallow-copy trap.
State your preference and why, rather than only describing clone().
interviewQuestions.title: Deep versus shallow cloning

commonMistakes: Checking the condition with if instead of while.
Calling wait or notify outside a synchronized block.
Using notify and waking a thread waiting on the wrong condition.
followUps: What goes wrong if you use notify() instead of notifyAll() here?
Why must wait() be called while holding the monitor?
When would you replace this with a BlockingQueue, and what do you lose?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: write a bounded producer-consumer buffer in plain Java using wait() and notifyAll(). Why must the condition be checked in a while loop, not an if?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Guard the buffer with synchronized methods, wait in a while loop when it is full or empty, and notifyAll after each change; the while loop protects against spurious wakeups and against another thread taking the item first.
tips: Write the while loop first and explain it before the rest.
Mention spurious wakeups by name.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: producer-consumer with wait and notify

commonMistakes: Capturing an argument when the expected object was already known.
Verifying every interaction instead of the one that defines the behaviour.
Stubbing with any() and then asserting nothing about the values.
followUps: When is a plain verify with an expected object better than a captor?
How does verifyNoMoreInteractions differ from verify with times(1)?
Why is stubbing a mock you then verify a smell?
interviewQuestions.question: Coding task: how do you test that a service saves exactly the right entity using Mockito, and when do you reach for an ArgumentCaptor instead of a simple verify?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Stub the dependencies, call the service, then verify the repository method was called once and capture its argument to assert on the saved fields; use a captor when the exact argument is built inside the method and you cannot construct it in advance.
tips: Explain the trigger first: the argument is built inside the method.
Keep one behaviour per test.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: verify behaviour with Mockito ArgumentCaptor

commonMistakes: Forgetting readResolve and creating a second instance on deserialization.
Thinking a private constructor alone makes a Singleton safe.
Using a Singleton for mutable global state that tests cannot reset.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A classic Singleton with a private constructor and a static instance looks safe, but it has three holes. Reflection can make the private constructor accessible and call it, producing a second instance; deserialization creates a new object without calling the constructor, so reading a serialized Singleton back gives you a second instance unless you add a readResolve method that returns the existing one; and cloning copies the instance unless clone is blocked. The usual defences are to throw from the constructor if an instance already exists, which stops reflection, to add readResolve, which stops deserialization, and to refuse cloning. The simpler and stronger answer is an enum with a single constant: the JVM guarantees one instance per classloader, serialization is handled by the language, and reflection cannot instantiate an enum, so all three attacks fail by construction. The trade-off is that an enum cannot extend another class and is awkward when construction needs parameters, in which case a static holder class with lazy initialisation plus the defences above is the fallback.
followUps: Why does readResolve fix the deserialization hole?
What breaks if you serialize a Singleton without readResolve?
When would you avoid a Singleton entirely, even a safe one?
interviewQuestions.question: How can a Singleton be broken in Java, and what is the most robust way to implement one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Reflection can call the private constructor, deserialization can create a second instance, and cloning can copy it; an enum singleton is immune to all three, which is why it is the most robust form.
tips: Name all three attacks, then give the enum answer.
Mention that enum singletons cannot extend a class.
interviewQuestions.title: How a Singleton breaks, and how to defend it

commonMistakes: Using an Abstract Factory for a single product type.
Letting callers mix products from different families.
Putting creation logic in the caller and calling it a factory.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Factory Method solves the problem of creating a single product: a creator class defines a method that returns a product, and each subclass decides which concrete product to build, so the calling code depends only on the product interface. Abstract Factory solves a bigger problem: creating a family of related products that belong together, such as a button, a text field, and a scroll bar that must all follow the same visual theme. It defines one factory interface with a creation method per product, and each concrete factory produces the whole matching set, so a caller cannot accidentally mix a dark-theme button with a light-theme text field. Choose Factory Method when you have one product type and the variation is which implementation is built; choose Abstract Factory when you have several related types and the variation is which consistent family is built. In Spring, a @Bean factory method is the everyday form of the first idea, while choosing between whole configuration families is the second idea in framework form.
followUps: What breaks if you mix products from two Abstract Factory families?
How does a Spring @Bean method relate to the Factory Method idea?
Why is the factory itself usually hidden behind an interface?
interviewQuestions.question: How do the Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns differ, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Factory Method creates one kind of object and lets subclasses decide the concrete type; Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related objects that must work together, such as a matching set of UI controls.
tips: Use one product versus a family of products as the dividing line.
Give a concrete family example, such as a UI theme.
interviewQuestions.title: Factory versus Abstract Factory

commonMistakes: Adding a builder to a two-field class.
Validating each field alone and missing invalid combinations.
Exposing the half-built object before build() is called.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A constructor with many parameters is hard to call correctly: callers mix up two Strings or two ints, and adding an optional field forces either a new constructor or a null argument. Telescoping constructors, where each constructor adds one more parameter, multiply quickly and still leave the caller guessing which argument is which.
