A builder fixes this by giving each field a named setter-like step, letting optional fields be left out, and producing an immutable object at the end through a single build step that can validate the whole combination. The cost is a second class, more code to maintain, and an object that is mutable during construction, so a builder is overkill for a small value object with two or three required fields, where a constructor or a record is simpler and clearer. In interviews, the honest answer names the threshold: roughly four or more parameters, or any case where two parameters share a type and could be swapped by mistake.
followUps: How does a builder help make an immutable object?
Where would you validate: in each builder step or in build()?
Why is a record sometimes a better answer than a builder?
interviewQuestions.question: When is the Builder pattern the right choice over constructors, and when does it become overkill?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a builder when an object has many parameters, several optional ones, or combinations that would need many constructors; skip it for small objects with two or three required fields, where a plain constructor is clearer.
tips: Name the threshold: four or more parameters, or same-type parameters that can be swapped.
Mention validation in build() as the place to check the whole combination.
interviewQuestions.title: Builder versus telescoping constructors

commonMistakes: Listing patterns without a Spring example for any of them.
Confusing a container-managed singleton bean with a hand-written Singleton class.
Calling every @Bean method a factory without explaining what it creates.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring is a good place to show pattern knowledge because the framework uses the patterns rather than just describing them. The IoC container is a factory: you ask for a bean by name or type and it decides which concrete class to build. Beans are singletons by default, with the container holding one shared instance per scope. AOP and @Transactional are proxies: the container wraps your bean so cross-cutting behaviour runs around your method. JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate are template methods: the framework owns the fixed steps, such as opening and closing resources, and you supply only the varying part. Adapters appear wherever Spring bridges two APIs, for example HandlerAdapter letting one dispatcher call controllers written in different styles. Naming the pattern is only half the answer; the senior version points at the concrete class or annotation in your own project and explains what would break if the pattern were removed.
followUps: Why are Spring singleton beans not the same as a Singleton pattern class?
How does a proxy change what happens when one bean method calls another?
Where does the Observer pattern appear in Spring?
interviewQuestions.question: Which design patterns does the Spring Framework itself use, and where can you point to each one in real code?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Spring is built on patterns: the container is a factory, beans are singletons by default, proxies add advice, templates handle boilerplate, and adapters bridge different APIs.
tips: Give the pattern and the Spring class together, not the pattern alone.
Use the proxy example to connect back to @Transactional behaviour.
interviewQuestions.title: Design patterns inside the Spring Framework

commonMistakes: Calling an @Async method from the same bean and expecting it to run in the background.
Using the default executor under load.
Letting exceptions from void @Async methods vanish silently.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Marking a method @Async and enabling async support makes Spring run it through a proxy on a thread from a TaskExecutor instead of the caller's thread, returning a Future or CompletableFuture you can compose. The default executor is a simple one that creates a new thread per task, so a production setup should define its own ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with a bounded queue, a named thread prefix, and a rejection policy, otherwise a burst of async calls can exhaust threads exactly like any other unbounded pool. The trap is the same proxy rule as @Transactional: the proxy only intercepts calls that arrive from outside the bean, so when one method of a bean calls its own @Async method, the call never reaches the proxy and the work runs synchronously on the caller's thread with no error to warn you. The fixes are the same too: call the async method through another bean, or inject the bean's own proxy. Exceptions also need care: a void @Async method that throws has no caller to receive the exception, so configure an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler to log it, or return a CompletableFuture so failures can be handled.
followUps: Why does a self-call run synchronously instead of failing loudly?
What should a production TaskExecutor configure that the default does not?
Where does a thrown exception go from a void @Async method?
interviewQuestions.question: How does @Async work in Spring, what executor does it need, and what goes wrong when an @Async method is called from the same bean?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Async runs the method on a separate thread through a proxy, so it needs a configured TaskExecutor and an external call; a self-call bypasses the proxy and runs synchronously on the caller's thread.
tips: Connect the trap to the proxy rule, not to async itself.
Name the executor configuration as a production requirement.
interviewQuestions.title: @Async, executors, and the self-invocation trap

commonMistakes: Creating beans unconditionally so consumers cannot override them.
Forgetting the properties prefix so settings collide with other starters.
Bundling a heavy dependency every consumer is forced to carry.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A custom starter has two parts: a small module that declares the dependencies a team always needs together, and an auto-configuration class that creates the beans for that setup. The auto-configuration is registered so Spring Boot can find it, and it is guarded by conditions: @ConditionalOnClass so it only applies when the library is present, @ConditionalOnMissingBean so a team's own bean wins, and @ConditionalOnProperty so the whole setup can be switched off. Configuration properties bind the team's settings from application properties with a clear prefix, and the starter should be ordered after the auto-configurations it depends on. The value for consumers is that a new service gets logging, metrics, security defaults, or client setup by adding one dependency instead of copying the same configuration class into every project. The risks to name are a starter that is too opinionated and hard to override, and a starter that drags in a heavy dependency every consumer must then exclude.
followUps: How does a team's own bean override a starter's bean?
How do you let a team switch a starter off without removing the dependency?
What makes a starter too opinionated to reuse?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you build a custom Spring Boot starter, and what does auto-configuration do for the teams that use it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A starter is a dependency that pulls in the libraries a team needs, plus an auto-configuration class that creates the beans only when its conditions match, so consumers get a working setup by adding one dependency.
tips: Describe the two parts first: dependency plus auto-configuration.
Name the three conditions as the mechanism that makes it safe.
interviewQuestions.title: Building a custom Spring Boot starter

commonMistakes: Assuming one @Transactional covers both databases.
Leaking the tenant key in a ThreadLocal across requests.
Forgetting @Primary and getting an ambiguous-bean failure at startup.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Spring Boot auto-configures a single DataSource, so a second database needs explicit beans: one DataSource, one EntityManagerFactory, and one transaction manager per database, with one of each marked @Primary so injection still works where only one is needed. To choose at runtime, for example per tenant, use AbstractRoutingDataSource, which picks the target DataSource from a key held in a ThreadLocal context that is set early in the request, usually by a filter or interceptor, and cleared afterwards so the thread does not leak the tenant into the next request. The hard part is transactions: a @Transactional method uses one transaction manager, so a write that touches both databases is two separate transactions and can commit in one and fail in the other. The honest answer is to avoid spanning databases in one transaction: keep each operation to one source, or accept eventual consistency with a saga or outbox. Also name the testing cost: each DataSource doubles the test setup, and a forgotten @Primary produces an ambiguous-bean error at startup.
followUps: Why must the routing key be cleared after the request?
What happens if you forget @Primary with two DataSources?
How would you handle a write that must touch both databases?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you configure multiple DataSources in Spring Boot, switch between them at runtime, and what breaks with transactions?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Define one DataSource bean per database, mark one @Primary, and route with AbstractRoutingDataSource driven by a context holder; transactions spanning both databases are not atomic, so keep each transaction to one source or use a saga.
tips: List the three beans per database before the routing part.
State plainly that cross-database transactions are not atomic.
interviewQuestions.title: Multiple DataSources and runtime routing

commonMistakes: Adding instances before checking whether the database is the bottleneck.
Raising the connection pool without checking what the database can handle.
Scaling a stateful service and splitting user sessions across instances.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start by finding the real bottleneck instead of guessing: check CPU, memory, thread-pool queue depth, database connection pool usage, and the slowest endpoints, and look at whether latency comes from the service, the database, or a downstream call. If the service itself is stateless, the fastest safe move is to add instances behind the load balancer, since a stateless service scales horizontally without code changes. Next protect the shared resources: raise the database connection pool only as far as the database can handle, add caching for hot read endpoints, and add timeouts and circuit breakers on downstream calls so a slow dependency cannot exhaust your threads. Then look at the code: add indexes for the slow queries, move heavy work off the request thread with async processing or a queue, and check for accidental per-request work such as repeated serialization or uncached lookups. Finally, make sure the change is safe to run: confirm sessions are not stored in memory on one instance, confirm the deployment can roll out without downtime, and set alerts on the metrics you just watched so the next doubling is caught earlier.
followUps: How do you know whether the bottleneck is the service or the database?
Why can raising the connection pool make things worse?
What breaks if the service keeps session state in memory?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your Spring Boot service must suddenly handle twice the traffic it was designed for. What do you do first, and what do you change next?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: First confirm where the bottleneck is with metrics and logs, then scale out behind a load balancer and protect the database with pooling, caching, and timeouts; only then tune the code, because scaling a bottleneck just moves it.
tips: Order the answer: measure, scale out, protect shared resources, then tune code.
Name one metric for each layer.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: doubling traffic on a Spring Boot service

commonMistakes: Adding an index without reading the plan first.
Testing the fix on a tiny dataset.
Fixing the query while the real problem is N+1 in the application.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start with the execution plan: EXPLAIN shows whether the database uses an index or scans the whole table, how many rows it expects to touch, and whether it sorts or joins in an expensive order. The usual causes are a missing index on the filtered or joined column, a query that defeats its index with a function on the column or a leading wildcard, a table that has grown past the point where the old plan works, or stale statistics that make the planner choose badly. Fixes follow the cause: add a covering index for the columns the query actually reads, rewrite the query so the filter can use the index, or update statistics and re-check the plan. Measure on realistic data volumes, because a query that is fast on a thousand rows can be slow on ten million, and check the fix under the same load, since an index that helps one query slows every write to the table. Also check the application side: an N+1 pattern, where one query per row replaces one joined query, often looks like a slow query but is really a slow loop.
followUps: How do you tell a missing index from stale statistics?
Why can an index that fixes a read hurt overall performance?
When is the real problem N+1 rather than the query itself?
interviewQuestions.question: A query that was fast is now slow in production. How do you find the cause and fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Run EXPLAIN to see the plan, check whether an index is used and how many rows are scanned, then fix the query or the index, and verify the plan changed on production-like data volumes.
tips: Start every answer with EXPLAIN.
Tie each cause to its fix.
interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing a slow query in production

commonMistakes: Adding a filter without a position and letting it land in a random spot.
Doing heavy work in a filter that runs on every request.
Assuming filters only run for controller requests.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Every request passes through a chain of servlet filters before it reaches a controller, and Spring Security owns that chain: one filter checks the security context, another handles login, another checks the user's roles against the URL, and another writes the security context back at the end. A custom filter, such as one that reads a token from a header and builds an authentication object, is added in the security configuration with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter, positioned relative to a filter whose job you understand, for example before the filter that checks authorization, so your authentication is in place when the check runs. Putting it in the wrong place is the classic bug: after the authorization check it never runs in time, and before the context filter it cannot rely on the security context existing. Filters are servlet-level, so they run for every request including errors and static resources, and they should do one small job and pass the request on quickly; heavy work in a filter slows every request. For debugging, enable security debug logging to see which filter rejected a request and why.
followUps: What happens if your filter runs after the authorization filter?
Why should a filter do only one small job?
How do you find out which filter rejected a request?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Spring Security filter chain, how do you add a custom filter, and where does it belong in the order?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Security is a chain of servlet filters that runs before your controllers; a custom filter is added with addFilterBefore or addFilterAfter relative to a known filter, and its position decides what it can see and what it can break.
tips: Explain position as the whole answer: before or after a known filter.
Name the classic bug: the filter runs too late.
interviewQuestions.title: Spring Security filter chain and custom filters

commonMistakes: Adding consumers beyond the partition count and expecting more throughput.
Ignoring rebalances as a cause of lag.
Assuming replication alone prevents data loss.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Consumer lag is the gap between the newest message and the last one a group has processed, and it is measured per partition, so the first step is to see whether one partition is stuck or all of them are behind. Common causes are slow processing in the consumer, too few consumers for the partition count, since a partition can only be read by one consumer in a group, and frequent rebalances, where a consumer joining or leaving stops the whole group while partitions are reassigned. Rebalances get slow when consumers take long to finish their current work or hold large state, and the fix is usually a mix of faster processing, more partitions, and the cooperative rebalancing protocol that moves fewer partitions at a time. When a partition leader fails, the cluster elects a new leader from the in-sync replicas, and consumers resume from there; the risk is the window where the leader accepted a write that no replica had copied yet, in which case that write is lost even though replication was configured. To shrink that window, require the producer to wait for all in-sync replicas before acknowledging, and keep the minimum in-sync replica count above one so a single replica cannot accept writes alone.
followUps: Why can a group not scale past its partition count?
What makes a rebalance slow, and what does cooperative rebalancing change?
How can data be lost even with replication enabled?
interviewQuestions.question: Your Kafka consumers are falling behind and rebalances take a long time. How do you diagnose it, and what happens when a partition leader fails?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Check lag per partition, slow processing, and rebalance causes first; add consumers up to the partition count or speed up processing, and remember a failed leader is replaced by an in-sync replica, but data can still be lost if the leader dies before replicas catch up.
tips: Start with lag per partition, not total lag.
Name the lost-write window explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Kafka consumer lag, rebalances, and broker failure

commonMistakes: Letting a choreographed saga grow until nobody can trace it.
Writing a compensating action that cannot safely run twice.
Treating a compensation as a database rollback.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A saga breaks a multi-service transaction into local steps, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. Choreography runs the saga without a boss: each service listens for an event, does its step, and publishes the next event, so the flow is defined by the services themselves. That is simple and loosely coupled for a short chain, but the overall flow is invisible: no one place shows the order, a missing event is hard to spot, and adding a step means changing several services. Orchestration puts one coordinator in charge: it calls each service in order, tracks which steps have completed, and runs the compensations in reverse when one fails. That makes the flow visible, testable, and easy to change, at the cost of a central service that every step depends on. Choose choreography when the flow is short, stable, and each service owns its part; choose orchestration when the flow is long, branches on results, or needs a clear audit trail. Either way, compensations must be idempotent, because a retry can run one twice, and every participant must handle duplicate events.
followUps: What breaks first when a choreographed saga grows to ten steps?
How does the orchestrator know which compensations to run after a failure?
Why must a compensating action be idempotent?
interviewQuestions.question: How do choreography and orchestration differ as ways to run a saga, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: In choreography each service reacts to events on its own; in orchestration one coordinator tells each service what to do. Choreography is looser and simpler for short flows, orchestration is clearer and easier to debug for long, branching flows.
tips: Contrast who holds the flow: nobody, or one coordinator.
Give the decision rule as flow length and branching.
interviewQuestions.title: Saga choreography versus orchestration

commonMistakes: Sharing one pool across all dependencies and calling it a bulkhead.
Sizing pools by guesswork instead of latency and traffic.
Queueing rejected calls instead of failing fast.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The pattern is named after a ship: watertight compartments keep one leak from sinking the whole vessel. In a service, the compartments are resource pools: each downstream dependency gets its own thread pool, its own database connection pool, or a semaphore limiting concurrent calls, so a slow payment service can exhaust only its own pool while the rest of the service keeps answering. In Spring Boot the usual implementation is a separate executor per client, or a resilience library's bulkhead that caps concurrent calls and rejects the excess fast instead of queueing it. The key difference from a circuit breaker is timing: a bulkhead limits damage while calls are still being attempted, whereas a circuit breaker watches failures and stops calling a dependency entirely for a while. They are usually combined: the bulkhead bounds the blast radius and the breaker stops the bleeding. The trap is sizing: a pool that is too small rejects healthy traffic, and one that is too large is no bulkhead at all, so size each pool from the dependency's latency and the traffic you expect, and expose pool usage as a metric.
followUps: How do you size a bulkhead pool for a dependency?
Why combine a bulkhead with a circuit breaker instead of choosing one?
What happens when a bulkhead rejects a call?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Bulkhead pattern, how do you implement it in a Spring Boot service, and how does it differ from a circuit breaker?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A bulkhead isolates resources per dependency, usually with separate thread pools or connection pools, so one slow dependency cannot consume everything; a circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency, while a bulkhead limits the damage while calls continue.
tips: Use the ship image, then the pool.
State the breaker difference as limit versus stop.
interviewQuestions.title: The Bulkhead pattern in practice

commonMistakes: Catching the exception instead of fixing the modification.
Assuming the exception is guaranteed to be thrown.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Most collection iterators are fail-fast: they record a modification count when created, and on every next() they check whether the count changed. If you add or remove elements inside a for-each loop, the count changes and the next call throws ConcurrentModificationException. Removing through the iterator itself is the exception: iterator.remove() updates the count, so it is safe. The other fixes are to gather the elements to remove in a separate list and apply the removal after the loop, to use removeIf, which is designed for exactly this, or to switch to a collection built for concurrent modification, such as ConcurrentHashMap or CopyOnWriteArrayList. Note that the exception is a best-effort detection aid, not a guarantee: it is thrown on a best-effort basis, so you must not write code that depends on catching it.
followUps: Why is Iterator.remove safe when list.remove inside the loop is not?
What does fail-fast actually guarantee?
interviewQuestions.question: What causes a ConcurrentModificationException, and how do you prevent it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It is thrown by a fail-fast iterator when the collection is structurally modified after the iterator was created, except through the iterator's own remove. Fix it by using Iterator.remove, collecting changes to apply after the loop, or using a concurrent collection.
tips: Explain the modification-count check; it demystifies the exception.
Offer removeIf as the idiomatic fix.
interviewQuestions.title: ConcurrentModificationException: why it happens and how to avoid it

commonMistakes: Assuming a record's List component cannot be mutated.
Using a record as a JPA entity.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Before records, a simple data class needed a constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString, most of it boilerplate that drifted out of sync. A record declares it in one line: record Point(int x, int y) {}, and the compiler generates a canonical constructor, accessor methods named x() and y() rather than getX(), and value-based equals and hashCode. Records are implicitly final, cannot extend another class, and their components are final, so a record is shallowly immutable: the reference cannot change, but a mutable object stored inside a record, such as a List, can still be mutated unless you defensively copy it. You can add validation in a compact constructor, which runs before the fields are assigned. Records are a poor fit for JPA entities, which need a no-arg constructor and mutable fields, and for anything that needs inheritance or mutable state. Use them for DTOs, API responses, and value objects.
followUps: How do you validate record components?
Is a record deeply immutable?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a record in Java, and when should you not use one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A record is a compact, immutable data carrier: the compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString from the declared components. Do not use one when you need mutable state, inheritance, or a JPA entity.
tips: Stress shallow immutability; it is the standard trap.
Name the fit: DTOs and value objects.
interviewQuestions.title: Records in Java: what they give you and where they do not fit

commonMistakes: Sealing a hierarchy that is meant to be extended by users.
Forgetting that permitted subclasses must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An ordinary abstract class can be extended by anyone, which makes exhaustive handling impossible: a switch over the hierarchy always needs a default branch for unknown future subtypes. A sealed class closes that hole: public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle {} names the only permitted subclasses, and each of them must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. The payoff comes with pattern matching for switch: the compiler knows the full set of subtypes, so it can prove a switch is exhaustive and reject it at compile time if a case is missing. That turns a runtime risk into a compile-time guarantee. Sealed classes are the right tool for fixed domain hierarchies such as expression trees, payment methods, or result types, and the wrong tool for hierarchies that are meant to be open for extension.
followUps: What must each permitted subclass declare?
How does sealing make a switch exhaustive?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a sealed class, and what does it buy you over an ordinary abstract class?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A sealed class declares exactly which classes may extend it, using permits; combined with pattern matching, the compiler can verify that a switch covers every subtype, so no default case is needed.
tips: Lead with the payoff: exhaustive switches checked at compile time.
Give a domain example, not just syntax.
interviewQuestions.title: Sealed classes: restricting the hierarchy

commonMistakes: Forgetting RUNTIME retention on an annotation a framework must read.
Putting an annotation where its @Target forbids it.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Every annotation you write is itself annotated with these two. @Retention has three values: SOURCE annotations exist only for the compiler, such as @Override, and are discarded; CLASS annotations are written into the bytecode but not necessarily loaded at runtime; RUNTIME annotations are available through reflection, which is what makes them useful to frameworks. @Target restricts the places the annotation may appear: TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, and others, so the compiler rejects an annotation placed somewhere meaningless. Spring's @Service is RUNTIME and TYPE, which is why component scanning can discover it by reflection. The common mistake is writing a custom annotation with the default CLASS retention and then wondering why reflection cannot see it at runtime. If a framework must read it, it must be RUNTIME.
followUps: What happens if a framework needs an annotation that is only CLASS retention?
How does Spring discover @Service at runtime?
interviewQuestions.question: What do @Retention and @Target control, and why does it matter which retention you pick?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: They are meta-annotations: @Retention says how long an annotation survives (source, class, or runtime), and @Target says where it may be used (type, method, field, and so on). Only RUNTIME annotations can be read by reflection, which is how frameworks like Spring find them.
tips: Give the three retention values as a ladder.
Tie it to a real framework example.
interviewQuestions.title: Annotations: @Retention and @Target

commonMistakes: Implementing State but letting the client pick states manually.
Using Strategy when behaviour must follow an internal lifecycle.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The two patterns look alike because both delegate behaviour to a separate object, but the intent is different. With Strategy, the client picks the algorithm: a payment service receives a PaymentStrategy, credit card or wallet, and calls it. The strategies do not know about each other, and the client controls the choice. With State, the object itself holds a state object and delegates to it, and the state decides the next transition: an order in NEW state accepts payment and moves to PAID, while a PAID order ships and moves to SHIPPED. The context does not choose; the state does. Strategy is the right answer when several algorithms do the same job and the caller should pick; State is the right answer when behaviour must change as the object moves through a lifecycle, and you want to replace a tangle of if-else on a status field.
followUps: How would you model an order lifecycle: Strategy or State?
What code smell tells you a State pattern would help?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the Strategy and State patterns?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Strategy lets the client choose an algorithm at runtime by injecting it; State lets the object change its own behaviour as its internal state changes, with the object choosing the next state. Strategy is about interchangeable algorithms, State is about behaviour that follows state.
tips: Use one contrast: client chooses versus object transitions itself.
Name the smell: if-else chains on a status field.
interviewQuestions.title: Strategy pattern versus State pattern

commonMistakes: Presenting the reflection hack as a legitimate technique.
Assuming the change is visible to all threads.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The trick works by getting the Field object, making it accessible, and then using reflection on the Field class itself to clear the FINAL bit from its modifiers, after which set() appears to work. The problem is that the Java Memory Model allows the JVM to treat final fields as constants: the compiler and JIT may inline the value into every place that reads it, so some code sees the new value and some keeps the old one, with no way to predict which. On top of that, the trick relies on internal APIs that the module system has closed off in modern JDKs, so it fails outright on recent versions. The interview point is the judgement: a candidate who knows the trick but explains why it is unsafe is far stronger than one who presents it as a clever hack. If you need a value to change, it should not be final.
followUps: Why might some code still see the old value after the change?
What does the module system do to this trick on modern JDKs?
interviewQuestions.question: Can you change a final field using reflection? What goes wrong if you try?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Technically yes on older JDKs by clearing the field's modifiers through reflection, but the JVM is free to inline final fields, so other code may keep seeing the old value, and modern JDKs block the trick entirely. Treat final as a real guarantee, not a suggestion.
tips: Lead with the inlining problem, not the trick itself.
End with the judgement: if it must change, it must not be final.
interviewQuestions.title: Changing a final field with reflection: possible, but a trap

commonMistakes: Using AtomicInteger for a check-then-act across two fields.
Assuming lock-free means contention-free.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The classic failure is i++ on a shared int: read, add, write is three steps, and two threads can interleave them and lose an increment. synchronized fixes it by serialising the whole operation, but the atomic classes fix it without a lock. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() uses a compare-and-swap instruction: read the current value, compute the new one, and write it back only if the value has not changed since the read; if another thread changed it first, the operation retries. Because there is no lock, a thread never blocks, which is why this is called lock-free. The limits are real: CAS works on one variable, so it cannot make two separate updates atomic together, and under heavy contention the retries can spin. For a compound update across several fields, or a check-then-act sequence, you still need a lock or a different design.
followUps: What is the ABA problem with compare-and-swap?
When would you still need synchronized instead of an AtomicInteger?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you ensure atomicity without using the synchronized keyword?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use the atomic classes such as AtomicInteger, which rely on compare-and-swap: a hardware instruction that updates a value only if it still holds the expected old value, retrying on conflict. It gives lock-free atomicity for single variables.
tips: Explain CAS as 'update only if unchanged, otherwise retry'.
Name the limit: one variable, not a compound update.
interviewQuestions.title: Atomicity without synchronized: Atomic classes and CAS

commonMistakes: Using TreeSet when only insertion order is needed.
Adding null to a TreeSet.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Both are sets, so both reject duplicates, but they organise elements differently. LinkedHashSet keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order, and get, add, and remove stay O(1) on average like HashSet. It also allows one null element. TreeSet keeps elements in a red-black tree ordered by natural ordering or a Comparator, so iteration is sorted and you can ask for subsets and ranges, but every operation costs O(log n), and a null element throws NullPointerException because null cannot be compared. The decision is therefore about what you need from iteration: insertion order means LinkedHashSet, sorted order means TreeSet, and neither order means plain HashSet. A practical note: LinkedHashSet is the usual answer for 'remove duplicates while preserving order', which is a common interview task.
followUps: How would you remove duplicates from a list while keeping the order?
Why does TreeSet reject null elements?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you use a LinkedHashSet, and when a TreeSet?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use LinkedHashSet when you need uniqueness plus insertion order with constant-time operations; use TreeSet when you need uniqueness plus sorted order, accepting logarithmic cost and no null elements.
tips: Frame it as a decision based on iteration order.
Give the deduplication use case for LinkedHashSet.
interviewQuestions.title: LinkedHashSet versus TreeSet

commonMistakes: Cloning shallowly and sharing mutable state between copies.
Using clone() without understanding its contract.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Instead of calling new and repeating a costly setup, you keep a ready-made prototype and clone it, then tweak the fields that differ. That is useful when creating an object involves heavy work such as loading configuration or building a complex graph, and you need many near-identical copies, for example document templates or game entities. In Java the mechanism is Object.clone() with the Cloneable marker, but clone is widely considered broken: it is protected, it does shallow copies by default, and it throws a checked exception. Modern code usually prefers a copy constructor or a copy factory method, which is explicit about what gets copied. The decision that matters is shallow versus deep: a shallow copy shares the referenced objects with the original, so mutating a list inside the copy mutates the original too, while a deep copy duplicates the whole graph and is the safe choice when the copies must be independent.
followUps: Why do many Java developers prefer a copy constructor over clone()?
When is a shallow copy dangerous?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Prototype pattern, and when is cloning better than creating a new object?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing one instead of constructing from scratch. It fits when construction is expensive or complex and you need many similar objects, and the key decision is shallow versus deep copying.
tips: Lead with the use case: expensive construction, many similar copies.
Name the shallow-versus-deep decision as the core of the answer.
interviewQuestions.title: The Prototype pattern: cloning instead of constructing

commonMistakes: Calling any wrapper a decorator.
Adding behaviour by changing the interface and calling it a decorator.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Both wrap an object, which is why they are confused, but their intent is opposite. An adapter exists because two interfaces do not match: InputStreamReader adapts a byte-based InputStream to the character-based Reader interface the client wants, and the client never sees the original interface. A decorator exists to add behaviour while keeping the interface identical: BufferedInputStream wraps an InputStream and adds buffering, and the result is still an InputStream that can be wrapped again. The test is simple: if the wrapper changes what the client calls, it is an adapter; if the wrapper can be stacked repeatedly and the client cannot tell it is wrapped, it is a decorator. Java's I/O library is the classic illustration of both in one place.
followUps: Which pattern is BufferedInputStream, and why?
Can the same class be both an adapter and a decorator?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the Adapter and Decorator patterns?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Adapter changes the interface of an existing class so it fits what the client expects; Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour around it. Adapter is about compatibility, Decorator is about enhancement.
tips: Use the java.io examples; they make the distinction concrete.
Give the test: does the interface change, or stay the same?
interviewQuestions.title: Adapter pattern versus Decorator pattern

commonMistakes: Logging through the implementation class instead of SLF4J.
Logging passwords or tokens.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The key idea is the facade: application code calls LoggerFactory.getLogger and logs through SLF4J, which is only an API. Spring Boot's default starter binds that API to Logback, so you get sensible console output and configuration through application.properties without writing any logging setup. To switch to Log4j2, exclude spring-boot-starter-logging from the web starter, add spring-boot-starter-log4j2, and provide a log4j2.xml or log4j2-spring.xml; because the code only depends on SLF4J, no logging call changes. Two practices matter more than the framework choice: use parameterized messages, log.info("Order {} placed", id), so the string is only built when the level is enabled, and never log sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, or full payloads containing personal data. For structured production logs, JSON layout and a correlation id in the MDC are the next steps.
followUps: Why is parameterized logging faster than string concatenation?
What should never appear in a log line?
interviewQuestions.question: How does logging work in Spring Boot, and how do you switch from Logback to Log4j2?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Code logs against the SLF4J facade, and Spring Boot binds it to Logback by default. Switching means excluding the Logback starter, adding spring-boot-starter-log4j2, and providing a log4j2 configuration file; your logging code does not change.
tips: Explain the facade first; the switch is then trivial.
Mention the sensitive-data rule.
interviewQuestions.title: Logging in Spring Boot: SLF4J, Logback, and switching to Log4j2

commonMistakes: Assuming scheduled tasks run in parallel by default.
Running a scheduled job on every instance without a distributed lock.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: fixedRate runs the task every N milliseconds measured from the start of the previous run, so runs can overlap in time if a run is slow, though with the default scheduler they simply queue. fixedDelay waits N milliseconds after the previous run finishes, so runs never overlap. cron gives full scheduling expressions such as 0 0 2 * * * for 2am daily. The gotchas are what interviewers probe: scheduling is single-threaded by default, so one long task blocks all other scheduled tasks, and the fix is to supply a TaskScheduler bean with a pool; scheduled methods must be void and parameterless; and a scheduled method that throws will log the failure and be retried on the next tick, which is fine for a polling job but bad for a task that must not skip. For work that must run exactly once across several instances, a scheduler alone is not enough: you need a distributed lock, for example with ShedLock.
followUps: How do you stop one slow scheduled task from blocking the others?
What happens if a scheduled method throws?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you run a scheduled task in Spring Boot, and what are the gotchas?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Enable scheduling with @EnableScheduling and annotate a method with @Scheduled using fixedRate, fixedDelay, or a cron expression. The default scheduler is single-threaded, so a slow task delays everything else.
tips: Contrast fixedRate and fixedDelay precisely.
Mention the single-threaded default as the gotcha.
interviewQuestions.title: Scheduling with @Scheduled in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Using hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN') and doubling the prefix.
Calling a secured method from inside the same class and expecting a check.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: URL rules in the filter chain are coarse: they guard paths, not business rules. Method security guards the operation itself, which matters when the same service method is reached from several endpoints. With @EnableMethodSecurity, you can write @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on an admin-only method, or @PreAuthorize("#order.customerId == authentication.name") to let a user touch only their own orders, using SpEL to reach the method arguments and the authenticated principal. @PostAuthorize checks the returned object instead, which is useful when the decision needs the result, for example returning an order only if it belongs to the caller. Two cautions: method security works through a proxy, so self-invocation inside the same class bypasses it, exactly like @Transactional, and hasRole automatically adds the ROLE_ prefix while hasAuthority does not, which is a common source of 403s that look like bugs.
followUps: Why does self-invocation bypass @PreAuthorize?
What is the difference between hasRole and hasAuthority?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you secure individual service methods in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Enable method security and annotate methods with @PreAuthorize, writing the rule as a SpEL expression such as hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.name; the check runs before the method body, and a failure produces a 403.
tips: Give a SpEL example that uses a method argument.
Warn about the self-invocation proxy trap.
interviewQuestions.title: Method-level security with @PreAuthorize and SpEL

commonMistakes: Keeping sessions in instance memory behind a load balancer.
Storing large objects in the session.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A session stored in one instance's memory breaks as soon as a load balancer sends the next request to a different instance, unless you pin users to instances with sticky sessions, which is fragile and defeats even load distribution. The clean answer is to avoid server-side state: issue a signed token such as a JWT, keep the state on the client, and let every instance verify it independently. When sessions are unavoidable, for example a legacy server-rendered app, Spring Session moves the session out of memory into Redis: spring-session-data-redis replaces the HttpSession implementation, every instance reads the same store, and the application becomes horizontally scalable. The trade-offs are a new dependency on Redis availability and the need to keep session contents small and serializable. Session fixation and timeout settings belong in the security configuration, not in application code.
followUps: Why are sticky sessions a bad long-term answer?
What breaks if you store a non-serializable object in a Spring Session?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you handle sessions in a Spring Boot application that runs on several instances?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Prefer stateless authentication with tokens so there is no session to share; if you must keep server-side sessions, externalise them with Spring Session backed by Redis so any instance can serve any request.
tips: Recommend stateless first, then Spring Session as the fallback.
Mention Redis as the shared store.
interviewQuestions.title: Session management and clustering in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Buffering without a bound.
Dropping items from a stream where loss is unacceptable.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In a blocking world, a slow consumer simply blocks the producer's thread. In a reactive pipeline there are no blocked threads, so the problem becomes explicit: a fast publisher can overwhelm a slow subscriber. The Reactive Streams specification solves this with demand: the subscriber requests N items, and the publisher must not send more than requested. Reactor builds on this with operators: onBackpressureBuffer queues excess items, which is safe only with a bound, because an unbounded buffer is just an out-of-memory error waiting to happen; onBackpressureDrop discards items the consumer cannot keep up with, which fits metrics and telemetry; onBackpressureLatest keeps only the newest item, which fits live dashboards. The design lesson is to choose the strategy from the data: financial transactions must never be dropped, so they need buffering plus a slow producer, while a sensor feed can drop. This is different from executor backpressure, which uses bounded queues and rejection policies on thread pools.
followUps: Which backpressure strategy fits a payment stream, and which fits a sensor feed?
Why is an unbounded buffer the worst option?
interviewQuestions.question: What is backpressure in reactive streams, and how do you handle a fast producer and a slow consumer?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Backpressure is the consumer telling the producer how much it can handle, using demand signals; in Reactor you handle overload with strategies such as buffering, dropping, or keeping only the latest item, and the worst choice is an unbounded buffer.
tips: Explain demand first: the consumer sets the pace.
Contrast with executor backpressure to show the distinction.
interviewQuestions.title: Backpressure in reactive streams

commonMistakes: Returning false for null inside a custom validator.
Writing validation logic in the controller instead of a constraint.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Built-in constraints such as @NotNull and @Size cover the common cases, but business rules need custom ones, for example a discount code that must match a pattern and exist in the catalogue. The recipe has three parts: an annotation that declares the message, groups, and payload and is meta-annotated with @Constraint(validatedBy = ...); a validator class implementing ConstraintValidator<YourAnnotation, String> whose isValid method returns false for bad values and true for null, because null is @NotNull's job; and the annotation placed on the DTO field. Spring Boot runs validation automatically when a controller parameter is annotated with @Valid, and failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException that a @ControllerAdvice turns into a 400 with field-level errors. A validator can also be a Spring bean, so it can inject a repository to check the value against the database, which is how existence checks are done.
followUps: Should isValid return true or false for null?
How do you validate a value against the database?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you write a custom validation annotation in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Define an annotation meta-annotated with @Constraint(validatedBy = YourValidator.class), implement ConstraintValidator with the isValid logic, and place the annotation on the field; Spring validates it automatically when the object is bound with @Valid.
tips: Give the three-part recipe in order.
Mention that null is @NotNull's job, not the validator's.
interviewQuestions.title: Custom Bean Validation in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Assuming a checked exception rolls back by default.
Raising isolation to SERIALIZABLE everywhere.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Propagation answers 'which transaction am I in?' REQUIRED, the default, joins the existing transaction or starts one if there is none, so the whole call stack commits or rolls back together. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction, starts a new one, and commits it independently, which is exactly what an audit log needs: the audit row must survive even if the business operation rolls back. NESTED runs inside the caller's transaction with a savepoint, so it can roll back alone. Isolation answers 'what can I see?': READ_COMMITTED sees only committed data, REPEATABLE_READ re-reads the same rows consistently, and SERIALIZABLE is fully isolated but slow. The default isolation comes from the database, and raising it is a performance cost, not a free correctness win. Two practical rules: only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback by default, so a checked exception needs rollbackFor, and @Transactional on a method only works when the call goes through the Spring proxy, so self-invocation silently runs without a transaction.
followUps: Why would audit logging use REQUIRES_NEW?
Why does calling a @Transactional method from inside the same class not start a transaction?
interviewQuestions.question: What do transaction propagation and isolation control, and when would you use REQUIRES_NEW?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Propagation decides whether a method joins the caller's transaction or starts its own, and isolation decides how much concurrent transactions can see of each other. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction and starts a fresh one, which is how you make audit logging survive a rollback.
tips: Use the audit-log example for REQUIRES_NEW; it is the canonical case.
Mention the unchecked-exception rollback rule.
interviewQuestions.title: Transaction propagation and isolation in Spring

commonMistakes: Returning entities directly from controllers.
Setting only one side of the relationship.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A bidirectional relationship means the parent holds a list of children and each child holds a reference back to the parent. Jackson follows references naively, so serialising the parent writes the children, each child writes the parent, and the cycle never ends until a StackOverflowError. The quick fixes are Jackson annotations: @JsonManagedReference on the parent side and @JsonBackReference on the child side tells Jackson to serialise the forward direction only, and @JsonIgnore simply drops the back reference. The better fix is architectural: do not return entities from controllers at all. Map to a DTO that contains exactly the fields the API promises, which also stops lazy-loading surprises and accidental data exposure. Two related rules: the owning side of the relationship is the one without mappedBy, and you should always set both sides of the relationship in code, using a helper method, or the in-memory object graph will disagree with the database.
followUps: Which side of a bidirectional relationship owns it, and how do you tell?
Why is returning a DTO better than a Jackson annotation here?
interviewQuestions.question: Why does returning a bidirectional JPA entity as JSON cause infinite recursion, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Because the parent serialises its children and each child serialises its parent, forever. Fix it with @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference, with @JsonIgnore, or, preferably, by returning a DTO instead of the entity.
tips: Explain the cycle first, then give the quick fix and the right fix.
Mention the helper method for keeping both sides in sync.
interviewQuestions.title: Bidirectional JPA relationships and infinite JSON recursion

commonMistakes: Enabling the second-level cache without an invalidation plan.
Expecting it to cache query results automatically.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Every Session has a first-level cache: within one session, loading the same entity twice returns the same object and no second query runs. The second-level cache extends that across sessions and across the application, so a second request for the same entity can skip the database entirely. It is configured per entity with @Cacheable and a cache concurrency strategy, and it needs a provider such as Ehcache or Hazelcast. It shines for reference data that is read constantly and changes rarely, such as countries or product categories. It hurts when the data changes often, because every write must invalidate the cached copy, and a stale cache is a correctness bug, not a performance problem. It also does nothing for queries: query results need the query cache enabled separately, and it is invalidated aggressively. The rule is to measure first, cache reference data only, and treat invalidation as part of the design.
followUps: What is the difference between the first and second level caches?
Why is caching write-heavy data usually a mistake?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the Hibernate second-level cache, and when does it hurt more than it helps?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The first-level cache is the persistence context, scoped to one session; the second-level cache is shared across sessions, backed by a provider such as Ehcache, and it helps read-heavy, rarely changing data while hurting write-heavy or frequently invalidated data.
tips: Contrast the two caches by scope first.
Name the fit: read-heavy reference data.
interviewQuestions.title: Hibernate second-level cache

commonMistakes: Adding indexes without ever reading a plan.
Trusting the estimated row counts without ANALYZE.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Guessing about performance is a waste of time; the plan is the evidence. EXPLAIN shows the execution plan the database chose, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds real timings. The things to look for are a sequential scan on a large table where an index should apply, which usually means the index is missing or the predicate does not match it; a large gap between estimated and actual rows, which means the statistics are stale and ANALYZE is needed; and nested loops over large inputs, which suggest a missing join index. The common reasons an index is ignored are a function wrapped around the indexed column, a type mismatch that prevents the comparison, or a query that returns most of the table, where a scan is genuinely cheaper. The workflow is: reproduce the slow query, read the plan, fix the cause, and re-run the plan to confirm the change.
followUps: Why would a database ignore an existing index?
What does a big gap between estimated and actual rows mean?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you use EXPLAIN to find out why a query is slow?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and read the plan: look for sequential scans on large tables, check the estimated versus actual row counts, and confirm the index you expect is actually being used.
tips: Describe the workflow: reproduce, read the plan, fix, confirm.
Name the function-on-indexed-column trap.
interviewQuestions.title: Using EXPLAIN to check whether a query uses an index

commonMistakes: Retrying against a service that is already down.
Returning an error as the fallback instead of a degraded answer.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A retry alone makes a failing dependency worse, because every client keeps hammering it. A circuit breaker stops the bleeding. In the closed state, calls pass through and the breaker counts failures; when the failure rate crosses a threshold over a window, it trips to open, and calls fail immediately with a fallback instead of waiting for a timeout. That fail-fast behaviour protects both sides: the caller gets a quick answer and the struggling service gets time to recover. After a configured wait, the breaker moves to half-open and allows a small number of trial calls; if they succeed, it closes and normal traffic resumes, and if they fail, it opens again. The tuning parameters are the failure threshold, the window, and the open-state duration, and the fallback must be a real degradation, such as cached data or a default, not an exception disguised as a response. Resilience4j is the usual implementation in Spring Boot, and it composes with retry and bulkhead.
followUps: How is a Circuit Breaker different from a Retry?
What should a fallback return?
interviewQuestions.question: How does a Circuit Breaker actually work, and what are its three states?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Closed means calls flow normally while failures are counted; when failures pass a threshold the breaker opens and calls fail fast without reaching the service; after a timeout it goes half-open, letting a few trial calls through to test recovery before closing again.
tips: Walk the three states in order; interviewers ask for them by name.
Stress fail-fast as the point of the pattern.
interviewQuestions.title: Circuit Breaker states: closed, open, and half-open

commonMistakes: Hardcoding service addresses in configuration.
Assuming client-side caching is always fresh.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Both solve the same problem: service addresses change as instances start and stop, so callers cannot hardcode them. With client-side discovery, the calling service queries the registry, caches the instance list, and chooses one, usually with a client-side load balancer. That gives the client control over load-balancing and failover, but every client needs registry logic and a cache. With server-side discovery, the client calls a fixed address, a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service, and that component resolves the instance. The client is simpler and needs no registry knowledge, but the load balancer is another component to run and a potential bottleneck. In practice, Kubernetes users get server-side discovery from Services almost for free, while Spring Cloud users historically used client-side discovery with Eureka; modern service meshes move the logic into a sidecar proxy, which is effectively server-side discovery per instance.
followUps: Which model does a Kubernetes Service use?
What is the downside of putting discovery logic in every client?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between client-side and server-side service discovery?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: In client-side discovery the client asks the registry and picks an instance itself, as with Eureka and a client load balancer; in server-side discovery the client calls a load balancer, which asks the registry and forwards the request, as with a cloud load balancer or Kubernetes Service.
tips: Frame it as: who picks the instance, the caller or a middleman?
Mention the service mesh as the modern convergence.
interviewQuestions.title: Client-side versus server-side service discovery

commonMistakes: Adopting a mesh for five services.
Assuming a mesh removes the need for application-level resilience.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: In a plain microservices system, every service reimplements the same concerns: encrypting traffic, retrying failures, emitting metrics, and routing canary traffic. A service mesh extracts all of that into a proxy, usually Envoy, injected as a sidecar container next to each service; application code makes plain calls to localhost, and the proxy handles the rest. The control plane, such as Istio or Linkerd, configures all the proxies centrally, so you can enable mutual TLS everywhere, split traffic for a canary release, or enforce a retry policy without changing any service. The cost is real: another layer to operate, more resource usage per pod, and a new set of failure modes to understand. The honest answer is that a mesh pays off when you have dozens of services and a platform team to run it, and it is unnecessary complexity for a small system where a gateway and good libraries are enough.
followUps: What does the sidecar proxy actually do for a service?
When would you not adopt a service mesh?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a service mesh, and when would you adopt one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A service mesh moves cross-cutting concerns such as mutual TLS, retries, observability, and traffic splitting out of application code into sidecar proxies next to each service, controlled centrally. It is worth it at scale, and overkill for a handful of services.
tips: Lead with the extraction idea: concerns leave the code.
End with the honest cost-benefit judgement.
interviewQuestions.title: What is a service mesh, and when is it worth it?

commonMistakes: Using the default groupingBy HashMap and losing the order.
Returning a null or a magic character when nothing repeats.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer:
The counting step needs a map that remembers insertion order, because the answer is the first character in the string whose total count exceeds one, not just any repeated character. Group the characters with Collectors.groupingBy, using a LinkedHashMap supplier and counting downstream, then stream the entries in order and pick the first with a count above one. The result is an Optional, because a string with no repeats has no answer, and returning Optional is honest about that. The whole pipeline is linear time with one map of distinct characters as extra space. Note that groupingBy with a custom map supplier is the detail most candidates miss: the default groupingBy returns a HashMap, which loses the order and can return the wrong character.

```java
public Optional<Character> firstRepeated(String input) {
    return input.chars()
            .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                    Function.identity(),
                    LinkedHashMap::new,
                    Collectors.counting()))
            .entrySet().stream()
            .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
            .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
            .findFirst();
}
```

Mention the alternative: a single pass with a HashSet that returns the first character seen twice is simpler and also linear, but it answers a subtly different question, the first character to repeat while scanning, which for most inputs is the same character.
followUps: Why must the map be a LinkedHashMap here?
Is there a simpler single-pass solution, and what does it change?
interviewQuestions.question: Given a string, find the first repeated character using Stream functions. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Count occurrences with a LinkedHashMap built through the stream, preserving first-appearance order, then return the first entry whose count is greater than one; if none exists, return an empty result.
tips: Point out the LinkedHashMap supplier; it is the key detail.
Return Optional instead of a sentinel value.
interviewQuestions.title: Coding: first repeated character with streams

commonMistakes: Scaling up before knowing what is saturated.
Adding caching before confirming the bottleneck is the database.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The order matters, because the wrong first move makes things worse. First, confirm it is a real traffic spike and not a retry storm from a failing downstream, by checking request rates, error rates, and downstream latency together. Second, protect the system: enable rate limiting, shed non-critical work such as recommendations or heavy reports, and scale horizontally if the service is stateless, which is why stateless design matters. Third, find the actual bottleneck instead of guessing: thread pool saturation, database connection exhaustion, a hot endpoint doing an N+1 query, or GC pressure each have different signatures in the metrics. Only then make the structural fix: cache the hot reads, move slow work to a queue, add database read replicas, or break the endpoint apart. After the incident, the follow-ups are autoscaling policies, load tests that reproduce the spike, and alerts on saturation metrics such as thread pool usage and connection pool wait time, so the next spike is caught before users feel it.
followUps: How do you tell a genuine traffic spike from a retry storm?
Which saturation metrics would you alert on?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your Spring Boot service's traffic suddenly triples and response times climb. What do you do, in order?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: First stabilise: confirm the spike is real, shed non-essential load, and scale out. Then find the bottleneck with metrics and profiling, and only then make structural changes such as caching, async processing, or a queue.
tips: Give the sequence: confirm, protect, diagnose, fix.
Name one metric per bottleneck type.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: handling a sudden traffic spike

commonMistakes: Using @Around for simple logging.
Forgetting that proceed() can throw the method's checked exceptions.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: @Before and @AfterReturning observe a call; only @Around controls it, because it receives a ProceedingJoinPoint and decides whether and when to call proceed(). That makes it the right tool for timing, retrying, caching a result, or short-circuiting a call. The risks follow from the power: forgetting proceed() means the method never executes and the caller gets whatever the advice returns; calling proceed() twice executes the method twice, which is dangerous for writes; and an @Around advice that swallows exceptions changes the method's contract silently. Prefer the narrower advice types unless you need to control the call.
followUps: How would you write a retry aspect with @Around?
Why is a broad pointcut dangerous?
interviewQuestions.question: When would you use @Around advice instead of @Before or @AfterReturning, and what can go wrong with it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: @Around is the only advice that wraps the call: it can time it, retry it, or replace its result. Forgetting proceed() skips the method; calling it twice runs it twice.
tips: Give the timing-aspect example, then name the two proceed() mistakes.
Say when you would not use @Around: pure logging belongs in @Before.
interviewQuestions.title: When to use @Around advice

commonMistakes: Using the passed-in object after merge() as if it were managed.
Calling persist() on a detached entity.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: When the persistence context closes, a managed entity becomes detached: Hibernate stops tracking it, so setter calls change the object but write nothing. merge() takes that detached state, loads or creates the corresponding managed instance, copies the state onto it, and returns the managed instance. The common bug is continuing to use the original reference — it is still detached, so further changes to it are silently lost. persist() is different: it makes a transient object managed, and throws if the object already has an identity.
followUps: How is persist() different from merge()?
Why does dirty checking not need an explicit save?
interviewQuestions.question: An entity is loaded in one transaction, modified after the transaction closes, and passed to merge(). What happens — and which object is managed afterwards?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: merge() copies the detached object's state onto a managed instance and returns it. The object you passed in stays detached; changes to it after the merge are ignored.
tips: Stress the return value: merge() returns the managed object; the argument stays detached.
Connect it to the four states: transient, managed, detached, removed.
interviewQuestions.title: Detached entities and merge()

commonMistakes: Treating StampedLock as a drop-in replacement for ReentrantLock.
Skipping validation and using a possibly stale read.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: StampedLock has three modes: write, read, and optimistic read. tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without acquiring any lock, so the read runs fully concurrently; afterwards validate(stamp) checks whether a write happened in between, and if it did, the code falls back to a read lock and re-reads. This is faster than a ReadWriteLock when writes are rare. The trap is reentrancy: unlike synchronized or ReentrantLock, acquiring a read or write lock twice in the same thread deadlocks, so StampedLock suits short, carefully written sections, not general-purpose locking.
followUps: When would ReadWriteLock beat StampedLock?
Why validate instead of just trusting the read?
interviewQuestions.question: How does a StampedLock optimistic read work, and what is its main danger?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: You take a stamp without locking, read, then validate(stamp): if a writer changed the data, validation fails and you retry under a read lock. The danger is that StampedLock is not reentrant — re-acquiring it in the same thread deadlocks.
tips: Explain the retry loop: optimistic read, validate, fall back to a read lock.
Name the non-reentrancy trap explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: StampedLock optimistic reads

commonMistakes: Saying a latch is reusable.
Using a barrier where a latch would do, or vice versa.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A CountDownLatch is created with a count; workers call countDown() as they finish and other threads block in await() until the count reaches zero. It cannot be reset — a second round needs a new latch. A CyclicBarrier makes N threads wait at a point until all N arrive, then releases them all together, optionally running a barrier action once; it resets automatically, so it fits repeated phases such as iterations of a parallel computation. A Semaphore is the third shape: permits limiting concurrent access to a resource, rather than coordinating timing.
followUps: What would you use to limit concurrent access to a pool of ten connections?
Can a CountDownLatch be reused?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a CountDownLatch and a CyclicBarrier, and when would you use each?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A latch is a one-shot countdown that waiting threads observe; a barrier is a reusable rendezvous where all parties wait for each other. Use a latch to wait for completion, a barrier for repeated phases.
tips: Answer by coordination shape first, class second.
Add the Semaphore contrast to show the family.
interviewQuestions.title: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier

commonMistakes: Treating ThreadLocal as free because virtual threads are cheap.
Using ThreadLocal for request context in a per-request virtual thread server.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: With platform threads, a ThreadLocal costs one copy per pooled thread — a small, bounded number. Virtual threads are cheap and numerous by design, so the same pattern multiplies the state by the number of live virtual threads, and values can linger as long as the virtual thread does. The replacement is to pass context explicitly as a method argument, or to use scoped values, which are designed for carrying immutable context across virtual threads without per-thread storage.
followUps: What is pinning, and how does it relate?
Would you use a thread pool for virtual threads?
interviewQuestions.question: Why is ThreadLocal dangerous with virtual threads, and what should you use instead?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: ThreadLocal state is per virtual thread, so a million virtual threads can mean a million copies of a value — a memory hazard. Pass context explicitly instead.
tips: Quantify it: bounded pool versus unbounded virtual threads.
Name scoped values as the intended replacement.
interviewQuestions.title: Virtual threads and ThreadLocal

commonMistakes: Saying the resource server calls the provider per request.
Accepting a token on signature alone.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A resource server does not ask the authorization server about each token. It fetches the provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint (published at /.well-known/jwks.json), caches them, and verifies the token's signature, issuer (iss), audience (aud), and expiry (exp) locally. In Spring Boot, setting spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri is enough: Boot discovers the JWKS endpoint from the provider's OpenID configuration and the framework's BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter does the validation before the request reaches a controller. A token with a valid signature but the wrong audience must still be rejected — signature alone is not enough.
followUps: What is the difference between a scope and a role?
Where would you configure the issuer URI?
interviewQuestions.question: How does a resource server validate a JWT without calling the authorization server on every request?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: It verifies the signature against the provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint, and checks issuer, audience, and expiry locally — the keys are fetched once and cached.
tips: Name the four checks: signature, issuer, audience, expiry.
Mention the issuer-uri one-liner — it shows you have configured one.
interviewQuestions.title: Resource server JWKS validation

commonMistakes: Sending the id_token as a Bearer token to an API.
Treating the id_token as proof of authorization.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The access token is what a client presents to a resource server: it carries scopes and is accepted as proof that the caller may do something. The id_token is an OpenID Connect JWT that states who the user is (subject, issuer, expiry, and profile claims) for the client that logged them in. An id_token is not an authorization credential for an API: the API cannot validate its audience or scopes, and accepting it would let a token minted for login authorize API access. Keep them separate — id_token for identity at the client, access token for authorization at the API.
followUps: What does the refresh token do?
How do scopes appear as authorities in Spring Security?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an access token and an id_token, and what goes wrong if you confuse them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The access token authorizes API calls; the OIDC id_token identifies the user. Sending an id_token to an API as a Bearer token is wrong — it was not issued for that API.
tips: One sentence each, then the failure mode.
Mention SCOPE_ prefix mapping for scopes.
interviewQuestions.title: Access token vs id_token

commonMistakes: Treating CAP as a one-time global choice.
Forgetting the latency half entirely.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: CAP says that during a partition a system chooses availability or consistency. PACELC adds the else: when there is no partition, the system chooses latency or consistency. Strongly consistent reads usually cost a round trip to the leader or a quorum; reading the nearest replica is faster but possibly stale. So a system can be PA/EL (available during partitions, low-latency reads otherwise, like a social feed), PC/EC (consistent in both cases, slower, like a bank ledger), or mixed per dataset — strong consistency for payments, eventual consistency for recommendations. The interview point is naming the trade-off per dataset and what breaks if you choose wrong.
followUps: Give an example of a PA/EL system and a PC/EC system.
How does Cassandra make this choice concrete?
interviewQuestions.question: What does PACELC add to CAP?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: CAP covers the partition case (availability vs consistency); PACELC adds the normal case (latency vs consistency), so the trade-off is made per dataset in both situations.
tips: Say the acronym out: Partition, Availability/Consistency, Else, Latency/Consistency.
Answer per dataset, not once for the whole system.
interviewQuestions.title: PACELC trade-offs

commonMistakes: Recommending a fixed window without naming the boundary burst.
Rate-limiting per instance in a multi-instance service.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Both bound the rate, but they treat bursts differently. A token bucket holds up to N tokens, refills at a fixed rate, and serves a request immediately if a token is available — so a user opening an app and firing ten requests at once is served, while the long-run rate stays bounded. A leaky bucket queues requests and drains them at a fixed rate, so bursts wait instead of being served, adding latency but giving the downstream system a perfectly smooth load. A fixed-window counter is simpler but allows double the rate across a window boundary; a sliding window counter fixes that with one counter per window. A distributed limiter needs shared state, usually Redis, or each instance enforces its own limit.
followUps: What status code and header should a rate-limited response carry?
Why does a per-instance limiter multiply the real limit?
interviewQuestions.question: Compare token bucket and leaky bucket rate limiting. When would you choose each?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity and bounds the long-run rate; leaky bucket smooths bursts into a fixed rate but queueing adds latency. Choose token bucket for bursty legitimate traffic, leaky bucket for a downstream that needs a steady rate.
tips: Compare on bursts: allowed versus smoothed.
Add the 429 with Retry-After detail — it is often the follow-up.
interviewQuestions.title: Comparing rate limiting algorithms

commonMistakes: Reading the ClassCastException as a type error.
Saying parent delegation means the child never loads anything.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Classes are loaded on demand by a hierarchy of loaders (bootstrap, platform, application, custom), and each loader asks its parent first before loading a class itself. That is why application code cannot shadow java.lang.String. A class is identified by its name plus the loader that defined it, so the same class loaded by two different loaders — for example, two web applications each loading their own copy of a library — is two different types, and casting between them throws ClassCastException even though the names match. The fix is to share the class through a common parent loader or communicate through an interface loaded by that parent.
followUps: What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?
When would you write a custom classloader?
