That gives frameworks two useful properties: the generated class cannot be accidentally referenced or subclassed by user code, and it can be unloaded independently when it is no longer needed, which matters for code that is generated repeatedly at runtime. The main consumers are the JDK itself, which generates lambda implementation classes as hidden classes, and frameworks that generate proxies or accessors. For an interview, the point is recognising the concept and its purpose, not the API: hidden classes are an infrastructure feature for generated code, not something application code creates directly.
followUps: Why can a hidden class be unloaded independently?
What in the JDK already uses hidden classes?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a hidden class, introduced in Java 15, and what is it used for?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A hidden class is a class that cannot be referenced by name: it is created at runtime through Lookup.defineHiddenClass, cannot be discovered by other classes, and is unloaded with its defining loader. Frameworks use them for generated code such as lambda bodies and proxies.
tips: Lead with the two properties: unfindable by name, independently unloadable.
Name lambdas as the concrete consumer.
interviewQuestions.title: Hidden classes in Java 15

commonMistakes: Declaring a counter volatile and believing it is thread-safe.
Treating visibility and atomicity as the same problem.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: These are two separate promises, and confusing them is the source of many concurrency bugs. Visibility is about memory: without synchronisation, a thread may keep a value in a register or a CPU cache and never see another thread's write, so a flag that stops a loop can appear stuck forever. volatile fixes this by forcing reads and writes to go to main memory and by establishing a happens-before edge. Atomicity is about indivisibility: i++ is three operations, read, add, write, and two threads can interleave them so that one increment is lost, even though every write is perfectly visible. volatile does nothing about that interleaving. The fixes are different: AtomicInteger gives atomic read-modify-write through compare-and-swap, and synchronized gives both visibility and atomicity for a block. The interview test is the counter: a volatile int counter incremented by many threads will finish with the wrong total, and the candidate must be able to say why.
followUps: Why does a volatile counter still lose increments?
What does synchronized give you that volatile does not?
interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between visibility and atomicity, and why does volatile fix only one of them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Visibility means a write by one thread is seen by others; atomicity means an operation completes as a single indivisible step. volatile guarantees visibility, but i++ is still a read-modify-write, so it is not atomic and can lose updates.
tips: Use the counter example; it makes the distinction undeniable.
Name the two fixes and what each provides.
interviewQuestions.title: Visibility versus atomicity in multithreading

commonMistakes: Picking ZGC because it is newest, without a latency requirement.
Tuning collector flags before measuring with GC logs.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The collectors differ in what they optimise. Serial uses one thread and is only right for small heaps or single-core machines. Parallel, the throughput collector, uses many threads and maximises the work done per second, at the cost of longer pauses, which suits batch jobs. G1, the default since Java 9, divides the heap into regions and collects the garbage-rich ones first, aiming for predictable pauses with good throughput, which suits most server applications. ZGC and Shenandoah are the low-latency collectors: they do most of their work concurrently with the application and keep pauses in the low milliseconds even on very large heaps, at the cost of more CPU and memory overhead. The defaults have changed over versions: Parallel was the default through Java 8, G1 took over in Java 9. The selection rule is simple: if you have a pause target in milliseconds, use ZGC or Shenandoah; if you have a throughput target, use Parallel; otherwise stay on G1 and tune only after measuring with GC logs.
followUps: Which collector was the default in Java 8, and what changed in Java 9?
What does a low-latency collector cost you in exchange for short pauses?
interviewQuestions.question: Which garbage collectors does modern Java offer, and how do you choose between them?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Serial for tiny heaps, Parallel for maximum throughput, G1 as the default balance since Java 9, and ZGC or Shenandoah when pause times must stay in milliseconds. Choose by the latency requirement, not by fashion.
tips: Organise by the trade-off: throughput versus pause time.
Mention the Java 8 to 9 default change.
interviewQuestions.title: Garbage collectors in modern Java: choosing between them

commonMistakes: Taking one thread dump and guessing from it.
Restarting the service and destroying the evidence.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Start by taking several thread dumps a few seconds apart: one dump shows a moment, several dumps show a pattern. A deadlock is easy to confirm: the JVM's deadlock detector, printed at the bottom of a jstack dump, names the threads and the locks in the cycle, and a thread that is BLOCKED on the same lock in every dump is a strong signal. Starvation is subtler: the thread is RUNNABLE but never progresses, which points to thread priorities being ignored, an unfair lock that always favours the same waiters, or, most commonly, a saturated thread pool where tasks queue forever behind long-running work. The fixes differ accordingly: a deadlock needs lock ordering or a redesign, starvation needs a fair lock, a bigger pool, or separating the long-running work onto its own pool. Also check the pool itself: a pool with a bounded queue and a CallerRunsPolicy can silently turn the submitting thread into a worker, which looks like starvation from the outside.
followUps: How do you tell starvation apart from deadlock in a thread dump?
What does CallerRunsPolicy do to the submitting thread?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you diagnose thread starvation and deadlock in a running production service?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Capture thread dumps with jstack or jcmd, look for BLOCKED threads and the locks they wait on, use the JVM's built-in deadlock detector, and distinguish starvation, where a thread never gets scheduled, from deadlock, where threads wait on each other forever.
tips: Insist on several dumps, not one; a pattern is the evidence.
Name the pool-exhaustion cause explicitly.
interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing thread starvation and deadlock in production

commonMistakes: Pooling every object indiscriminately.
Optimising allocation without profiling first.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Garbage collection pauses are proportional to how much garbage you create, so the design goal is allocation rate, not heap size. The techniques are concrete: keep hot-path data in primitive arrays instead of boxed collections, reuse buffers and builders instead of allocating per request, avoid string concatenation and temporary objects inside tight loops, and prefer immutable value objects only where they are cheap. Object pooling is sometimes suggested, but it is a trade-off: it adds complexity and can hurt the generational collector's assumptions, so it is worth it only for expensive objects such as large buffers or connections. On the collector side, a low-latency collector such as ZGC tolerates the remaining allocation, and the JVM's escape analysis can already eliminate some allocations by keeping short-lived objects on the stack. None of this should be done blindly: profile allocation with a tool such as async-profiler or JFR, fix the top allocators, and measure again.
followUps: Why can object pooling sometimes make GC worse?
How would you find the top allocating code in a running service?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you build a high-performance system that creates as little garbage as possible?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Reduce allocation at the hot path: reuse objects where safe, prefer primitives and arrays over boxed collections, avoid temporary objects in loops, and pick a low-latency collector; then prove it with allocation profiling, because guessing about allocation is usually wrong.
tips: Frame the goal as allocation rate, not heap size.
Warn against pooling as a reflex.
interviewQuestions.title: Designing a system that needs minimal garbage collection

commonMistakes: Benchmarking a JVM without warm-up and trusting the numbers.
Disabling the JIT in production to 'simplify' things.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Java's performance comes from this adaptive design. Code starts interpreted, which is slow but has no warm-up cost, while the JVM counts method calls and loop iterations. Hot methods are compiled first by C1, a fast compiler that produces decent native code quickly, and the hottest methods are recompiled by C2 with aggressive optimisations such as inlining, escape analysis, and loop unrolling. This tiered compilation is the default. Compilation is speculative: the JIT optimises for what it has observed, and if an assumption later breaks, for example a method that was always called with one type suddenly receives another, the code is deoptimised back to the interpreter and recompiled. That is why benchmarks need warm-up, and why the first requests after a deploy are slower. Disabling the JIT with -Xint, or disabling tiered compilation, is only useful for debugging a suspected JIT bug; in production it can make the application several times slower.
followUps: Why are the first requests after a deploy slower?
What is deoptimisation, and when does it happen?
interviewQuestions.question: How does the JIT compiler work in the JVM, and what happens if you disable it?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode, profiles the hot methods, and compiles them to native code with the C1 and C2 compilers in tiers; disabling the JIT with -Xint makes everything interpreted, which is dramatically slower and only useful for debugging.
tips: Tell the story in order: interpret, profile, compile, deoptimise.
Explain warm-up as a consequence of the design.
interviewQuestions.title: How the JIT compiler works, and when you would disable it

commonMistakes: Trying to absorb the attack in application code alone.
Holding threads on slow downstream calls during an attack.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The application layer is the last line, not the first. Most of the defence lives in front of the service: a CDN absorbs static traffic, a web application firewall blocks known attack patterns, and rate limiting at the API gateway or load balancer caps requests per client, which is where a distributed attack is cheapest to stop. What the application itself must do is fail cheaply and stay responsive: set short timeouts on downstream calls so a slow dependency does not hold threads, limit connection pools and request sizes, reject malformed requests before they reach business logic, and use a token-bucket limiter such as Bucket4j for expensive endpoints. Equally important is observability: alert on request rate and error rate anomalies so the attack is noticed in minutes, and have a runbook for enabling stricter limits or blocking a source. No single layer stops a large attack; the layers together buy time and keep the service usable for legitimate users.
followUps: Where is the cheapest place to stop a DDoS attack?
Why is a timeout a defence, not just a convenience?
interviewQuestions.question: What is a DDoS attack, and how do you defend a Spring Boot application against one?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: A DDoS attack overwhelms the service with traffic from many sources. Defence is layered: a CDN or WAF and rate limiting at the edge absorb most of it, and the application adds timeouts, connection limits, and cheap rejection of bad requests so legitimate traffic still gets through.
tips: Stress the layering: edge first, application second.
Name a concrete limiter for expensive endpoints.
interviewQuestions.title: Defending a Spring Boot application against DDoS attacks

commonMistakes: Forgetting RUNTIME retention, so nothing can read the annotation.
Expecting the annotation to execute code by itself.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: An annotation is declared with @interface and its elements look like methods with defaults: @interface LogExecutionTime { boolean enabled() default true; }. Two meta-annotations matter: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME), without which nothing can read it at runtime, and @Target, which restricts where it may be placed, for example ElementType.METHOD. The annotation itself does nothing; something must read it. The common patterns are an Aspect with a @Around pointcut matching @annotation(LogExecutionTime), which logs timing without touching business code, and a BeanPostProcessor that inspects beans at startup, for example to register methods as handlers. A frequent mistake is putting the annotation on a method that is called from inside the same class: the AOP proxy is bypassed, so the advice never runs, exactly as with @Transactional. Keep annotations for cross-cutting metadata, not for business rules that belong in code.
followUps: Why does the annotation do nothing on its own?
Why would an annotation on a self-invoked method never trigger?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you create and use a custom annotation in Spring Boot?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Declare it with @interface, give it RUNTIME retention and a @Target, then process it: either with Spring AOP for behaviour such as logging, or by reading it at startup with reflection or a BeanPostProcessor.
tips: Give the three parts: declare, retain at runtime, process it.
Mention the self-invocation proxy trap.
interviewQuestions.title: Creating a custom annotation in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Declaring success because the deploy job went green.
Watching averages instead of percentiles.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A successful deploy is not a successful release. The verification sequence is: first, confirm the new instances are actually serving traffic, through health and readiness endpoints and load balancer registration; second, run a small set of smoke tests that exercise the critical paths, login, the main API calls, and the payment flow, against production; third, watch the metrics that matter for at least one business cycle, comparing error rate, latency percentiles, and saturation against the pre-deploy baseline, because averages hide regressions that p99 reveals. Set explicit rollback triggers before the deploy, for example error rate above 1% for five minutes, and make sure the rollback is a single action, not a rebuild. Feature flags make this safer still: the code ships dark, the flag is enabled for a small percentage, and the blast radius stays small if the verification fails.
followUps: Why is p99 more useful than the average latency here?
What makes a rollback trigger explicit rather than a gut feeling?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: you have just deployed a new version to production. How do you verify it is healthy before declaring success?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Check health endpoints and error rates, run smoke tests against real traffic paths, compare key metrics with the pre-deploy baseline, and keep the rollback ready with a clear trigger; do not declare success because the deploy finished.
tips: Separate 'deploy finished' from 'release healthy'.
Name the rollback trigger as a number, not a feeling.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: verifying a deployment in production

commonMistakes: Testing everything with @SpringBootTest and a slow suite nobody runs.
Using an in-memory database that behaves differently from production.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The pyramid exists because each layer has a different cost. Unit tests for services and domain logic are fast and precise, and they should be the majority. Slice tests use Spring's test slices: @WebMvcTest for controllers with mocked services, and @DataJpaTest for repositories against an in-memory or container database, which test the layer's real wiring without starting the whole application. Full @SpringBootTest tests are the slowest and most brittle, so reserve them for the paths that genuinely need the whole context, such as startup configuration and security. For anything that touches a real database, queue, or external service, Testcontainers gives you the real dependency in a container, which removes a whole class of 'works on my machine' failures. At service boundaries, contract tests verify that a provider still honours what its consumers expect, which is cheaper than end-to-end tests and catches the breaking change at the source.
followUps: Why are slice tests preferable to @SpringBootTest for a controller?
What problem do Testcontainers solve that an in-memory database does not?
interviewQuestions.question: What testing strategy do you recommend for a Spring Boot application?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Follow the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer slice tests for the web and data layers, and a small number of full integration tests with Testcontainers, with contract tests at service boundaries.
tips: Structure the answer as the pyramid, bottom to top.
Name one slice annotation per layer.
interviewQuestions.title: Testing strategy for a Spring Boot application

commonMistakes: Renaming a column in the same release as the code change.
Running a locking migration against a live table.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The problem is that the old and new versions of the application run side by side during a rolling deploy, so the schema must work for both. Expand-and-contract solves this in three releases. First, expand: add the new column as nullable, or add the new table, in a migration that changes nothing the old code depends on. Second, deploy the new code that writes to both the old and the new shape and reads from the new one. Third, contract: once the old code is gone, drop the old column or table in a separate release. The traps are renames and type changes, which break the old code immediately, and long-running migrations that lock the table, such as adding a column with a default on a huge table or building an index without CONCURRENTLY in Postgres. Flyway or Liquibase version the migrations, but they do not make an unsafe migration safe: the safety comes from the pattern and from testing the migration against a production-sized copy first.
followUps: Why must a column rename be done in two releases?
What makes a migration lock a table, and how do you avoid it?
interviewQuestions.question: How do you change a production database schema without downtime?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use the expand-and-contract pattern: first deploy a backward-compatible change that both old and new code tolerate, then deploy the new code, then remove the old shape in a later release; never run a locking migration against a live table.
tips: Walk the three phases in order.
Name the rename as the classic breaking change.
interviewQuestions.title: Zero-downtime database migrations

commonMistakes: Using field injection because it is shorter.
Reaching for the ApplicationContext in application code.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Field injection with @Autowired on a private field is the most common form in tutorials and the worst in production: the dependencies are invisible in the constructor, the fields cannot be final, the class cannot be instantiated in a plain unit test without reflection, and the container must use reflection to set them. Constructor injection fixes all of that: the dependencies are explicit parameters, the fields are final, and a test constructs the object with new. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor is autowired automatically, so no annotation is needed. For the cases field injection seems to solve, there are better tools: @Bean methods in a @Configuration class for wiring third-party classes, ObjectProvider<T> when a dependency is optional or should be resolved lazily, and @Lookup for prototype beans. Getting a bean from the ApplicationContext directly works but hides the dependency and couples the code to the container, so treat it as a last resort for framework code, not application code.
followUps: How do you inject an optional dependency without field injection?
Why can a constructor-injected class be tested without Spring?
interviewQuestions.question: What are the alternatives to @Autowired, and why is field injection discouraged?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Prefer constructor injection, which needs no annotation on a single constructor and makes dependencies explicit and immutable; other options are @Bean methods, ObjectProvider for optional or lazy dependencies, and direct ApplicationContext lookups, which should be a last resort.
tips: Lead with the testability argument; it is the strongest one.
Mention that a single constructor needs no annotation.
interviewQuestions.title: Alternatives to @Autowired field injection

commonMistakes: Making downstream calls with no timeout.
Retrying without backoff or a limit.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: RestTemplate is the old blocking client: simple and familiar, but each call holds a thread, and it is in maintenance mode, so no new features are coming. WebClient is its replacement: non-blocking and reactive, so one thread can serve many in-flight calls, which matters when a service fans out to several others. Feign is declarative: you write an interface with annotations, and Spring Cloud generates the client, including load balancing and, with Resilience4j, a circuit breaker. The client choice is less important than the resilience around it: every call needs a connection timeout and a read timeout, or a slow downstream will exhaust your thread pool; retries need backoff and a limit, or they amplify an outage; a circuit breaker stops calls to a service that is already down; and a correlation id must be propagated in headers, or a request cannot be traced across services. A call without a timeout is the most common production failure in this area.
followUps: Why is a call without a timeout so dangerous?
When would you choose WebClient over Feign?
interviewQuestions.question: How should one microservice call another, and how do RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign differ?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use a declarative client such as Feign or a non-blocking WebClient for new code; RestTemplate is blocking and in maintenance mode. Whichever you pick, add timeouts, retries with backoff, a circuit breaker, and propagate correlation ids.
tips: Compare the three clients in one pass, then pivot to resilience.
Name the timeout as the most common production failure.
interviewQuestions.title: Service-to-service calls: RestTemplate, WebClient, and Feign

commonMistakes: Deciding by seniority instead of by criteria.
Letting the argument run until the sprint fails.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The lead's job is not to pick the cleverer design; it is to unblock the team. Start by listening to each person separately, because in a group argument people defend positions rather than explaining reasoning. Then reframe the disagreement around criteria the team can agree on: what does each option cost in complexity, risk, and time, and what does the decision need to be reversible or not. If the decision is easily reversible, decide fast and revisit later; if it is hard to reverse, spend the time to prototype or spike the risky part. Make the decision explicit, name who owns it, write down the reasoning and the trade-offs, and set a date to revisit it if the assumptions change. What the lead must not do is decide by seniority, let the argument run until the sprint fails, or pretend a compromise that satisfies nobody is a decision. A team that sees decisions made cleanly and revisited honestly will argue less the next time.
followUps: How do you decide when a technical disagreement needs a prototype?
What do you do if the same disagreement keeps coming back?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: two developers on your team disagree strongly about a technical approach and the argument is blocking the sprint. As the lead, what do you do?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Separate the people from the problem: hear each side privately, agree on the decision criteria and who decides, make a decision with a time-box for revisiting it, and document it so the team can move on without relitigating it.
tips: Give the sequence: listen separately, agree criteria, decide, document.
Distinguish reversible from irreversible decisions.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: handling conflict within your team as a lead

commonMistakes: Cutting testing to meet the date.
Accepting every new request after the plan is set.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The first step is to make the work visible: list everything, estimate it honestly, and sort by the value delivered and the risk of not doing it, not by who shouted loudest. Then cut scope, not quality: a smaller feature that works is worth more than a larger one shipped broken, and quality cuts become production incidents that cost more than the time saved. Present the choice to stakeholders as options with consequences, for example 'we can ship X and Y by Friday, or X, Y, and Z two weeks later', because a trade-off presented as options gets a decision, while a complaint about workload gets sympathy and no decision. Once the plan is agreed, freeze it: every new request goes through the same ranking, or the team spends the sprint re-planning instead of building. Finally, say what is being dropped out loud, in writing, so nobody is surprised at the deadline, and protect the team's focus by being the person who says no.
followUps: How do you present a scope cut to stakeholders so it gets accepted?
When is it right to push back on a deadline instead of cutting scope?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your team has more work than it can finish before a hard deadline. How do you prioritise?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Rank by business impact and risk, cut scope before cutting quality, make the trade-off visible to stakeholders with options rather than a single plea for more time, and protect the team from thrash by freezing the plan once it is set.
tips: Give the options-with-consequences framing.
Mention freezing the plan after the decision.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: prioritising work under tight deadlines and limited resources

commonMistakes: Starting a big-bang rewrite with no tests.
Refactoring code nobody needs to change.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A big-bang rewrite is the classic trap: it takes months, the new system must reproduce undocumented behaviour the old one accumulated, and the business gets nothing until the end. The safer approach starts with understanding: read the code, talk to the people who run it, and find the seams where it can be tested. Then add characterization tests, tests that capture what the code actually does today, not what it should do, around the area you are about to change, so a change that breaks behaviour is caught immediately. Change incrementally, leaving each area slightly better than you found it, and use the strangler pattern for larger pieces: route new behaviour through new code while the old code keeps serving the rest. Rewrite only the piece you can prove is cheaper to replace than to fix, and only when a business change gives you the reason and the budget.
followUps: What is a characterization test, and how is it different from a unit test?
When is a rewrite actually the right call?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: you inherit a large legacy codebase with no tests and fragile behaviour. What is your approach?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Do not rewrite it: first make it safe to change with characterization tests around the code you must touch, then improve it incrementally with the boy-scout rule, and extract or replace pieces only when a business change forces you to.
tips: Lead with 'do not rewrite it'; it is the expected judgement.
Explain characterization tests as the safety net.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: taking over a legacy codebase

commonMistakes: Logging personal data in plain text.
Storing data you do not need 'just in case'.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: Privacy is a design concern, not a checkbox at the end. Start with minimisation: collect only the data the feature needs, and do not store what you do not need, because data you do not hold cannot leak. Protect what you keep: TLS in transit, encryption at rest for sensitive fields, and secrets in a vault rather than in configuration or code. Restrict access by role and by need, and audit who accessed what, because most breaches involve legitimate access used wrongly. Keep personal data out of logs and error messages, where it is routinely copied into systems with weaker controls, and mask it in non-production environments. Know the rules that apply: retention periods, the right to deletion, and consent requirements under regulations such as GDPR and India's DPDP Act, and design the deletion path before launch, because deleting a user's data from backups, caches, and analytics is the part teams forget until a request arrives.
followUps: Why is data minimisation the strongest privacy control?
How do you handle a user's deletion request across backups and caches?
interviewQuestions.question: Scenario: your service handles personal data. How do you handle privacy and security as a senior developer?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Minimise what you collect, encrypt sensitive data in transit and at rest, restrict access to the minimum needed, keep personal data out of logs, and know the retention and deletion rules that apply to your users.
tips: Start with minimisation; it frames everything else.
Mention logs as the place personal data leaks most often.
interviewQuestions.title: Scenario: handling data privacy and security in your projects
Distributed ID generation
interviewQuestions.question: How would you generate unique IDs across many machines without coordination, and what are the trade-offs?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Use time-ordered UUID v7 for coordination-free ordered IDs, or Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + worker id + sequence) when IDs must be compact 64-bit numbers — accepting the need for unique worker ids and clock discipline.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: A database sequence is simple and ordered but a single point of contention. Random UUID v4 needs no coordination but is unordered, so database indexes fragment. UUID v7 adds a timestamp prefix, giving roughly time-ordered IDs with no coordination — the modern default. Snowflake-style IDs pack a timestamp, a worker id, and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits: ordered, compact, and sortable, at about 4,096 IDs per millisecond per worker — but worker ids must be unique (assigned at startup) and a clock moving backwards can duplicate IDs. Choose by the requirement: sortable (Snowflake or UUID v7), unpredictable (random UUIDs, which do not leak creation order or volume), or no coordination at all (UUIDs, not a sequence).
followUps: Why are random UUIDs bad as a clustered primary key?
How do you assign Snowflake worker ids?
tips: Start from the requirement: sortable, unpredictable, or coordination-free.
Give the Snowflake bit layout: 41 timestamp, 10 worker, 12 sequence.
commonMistakes: Using sequential IDs for public resources, leaking order and volume.
Using random UUIDs as a clustered key and wondering why inserts are slow.

interviewQuestions.title: Diagnosing OutOfMemoryError
interviewQuestions.question: Your service throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space in production. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.shortAnswer: Read the message, capture a heap dump with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, find the biggest retainer with a histogram and dominator tree, and fix the retention — not the heap size.
interviewQuestions.detailedAnswer: The message names the resource, and each one has a different fix: heap space means live objects fill the heap, GC overhead limit means the collector is spending almost all its time recovering almost nothing, Metaspace means class metadata, and unable to create a new native thread means too many threads, not too little heap. For heap space, enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError (with a HeapDumpPath) so the dump is captured at the moment of failure, look at jmap -histo to see which classes dominate, then open the dump in an analyzer and follow the dominator tree to the retainer — usually one collection holding references the application forgot. Raising -Xmx helps only if the application genuinely needs more heap; for a retention leak it delays the same crash. GC logs show whether the heap grew steadily (a leak) or spiked (a burst).
followUps: How do you tell a leak from a workload spike?
What would you do for OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread?
tips: Give the sequence: message, dump, histogram, dominator tree, retainer.
Say when raising -Xmx is right — genuinely more live data — and when it is not.
commonMistakes: Answering 'increase the heap' with no diagnosis.
Restarting without capturing a dump.
